(iii) A spherical wavefront converging towards the focus of the mirror. [½]
(iv) A plane wavefront tilted (towards the base of the prism), because the part passing through the thicker base is delayed more. [½]

items.q: Using Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV for the hydrogen atom, find (i) the shortest wavelength (series limit) of the Balmer series, (ii) the shortest wavelength (series limit) of the Paschen series. Name the region of the spectrum in which each lies. (hc = 1240 eV nm)
items.ans:
(i) Balmer series limit: n = ∞ → 2, ΔE = 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV; λ = 1240/3.4 ≈ 365 nm — near ultraviolet (just beyond the violet end of the visible). [1]
(ii) Paschen series limit: n = ∞ → 3, ΔE = 13.6/9 ≈ 1.51 eV; λ = 1240/1.51 ≈ 821 nm — infrared. [1]

items.q: Distinguish between the diffusion current and the drift current in a p-n junction. Which of the two is dominant (i) when the junction is forward biased, (ii) when it is reverse biased?
items.ans:
Diffusion current is due to majority carriers moving from the region of higher concentration to lower concentration (holes p → n, electrons n → p). Drift current is due to minority carriers swept across the junction by the electric field of the depletion region; the two flow in opposite directions and are equal in an unbiased junction. [1]
(i) Forward bias lowers the barrier, so diffusion current (of the order of mA) dominates. (ii) Reverse bias raises the barrier and stops diffusion, so only the small drift current (μA) flows. [1]

items.q: An electron enters the region between two parallel charged plates with a speed of 2.0×10⁶ m/s, moving parallel to the plates. The uniform electric field between the plates is 200 N/C and the plates are 5.0 cm long. Find the vertical deflection of the electron when it leaves the plates, and state the shape of its path between the plates. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg)
items.ans:
Acceleration perpendicular to the plates a = eE/m = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 200/9.1×10⁻³¹ ≈ 3.5×10¹³ m/s²; time between the plates t = L/v = 0.05/2×10⁶ = 2.5×10⁻⁸ s. [1]
Deflection y = ½at² = ½ × 3.5×10¹³ × (2.5×10⁻⁸)² ≈ 1.1×10⁻² m ≈ 1.1 cm (towards the positive plate). Since the velocity along the plates is constant while the motion perpendicular to them is uniformly accelerated, the path is a parabola (y = eEx²/2mv²). [1]

items.q: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 6.0 cm is to be used to cancel the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field (0.35×10⁻⁴ T) at its centre. Find the current needed. How should the plane of the coil be placed? (μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
items.ans:
At the centre B = μ₀NI/2r. Setting B = B_H: I = 2rB_H/(μ₀N) = (2 × 0.06 × 0.35×10⁻⁴)/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 50) ≈ 6.7×10⁻² A ≈ 67 mA. [1]
The field of the coil at its centre is along its axis, so the axis must lie along the magnetic meridian (north–south): the coil stands in a vertical east–west plane, with the current sense chosen so that its field at the centre points south, opposite to B_H. [1]

items.q: Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm in air enters water of refractive index 1.33. Find (i) the speed of the light in water, (ii) its wavelength and frequency in water. (c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
items.ans:
(i) v = c/μ = 3×10⁸/1.33 ≈ 2.26×10⁸ m/s. [1]
(ii) The frequency does not change on refraction: ν = c/λ = 3×10⁸/589×10⁻⁹ ≈ 5.09×10¹⁴ Hz. Wavelength in water λ_w = λ/μ = 589/1.33 ≈ 443 nm. [1]

items.q: Neutrons in thermal equilibrium at room temperature ('thermal neutrons') have a kinetic energy of about 0.025 eV. Find the de Broglie wavelength of such a neutron. Why are thermal neutrons suitable for studying the arrangement of atoms in a crystal? (m_n = 1.675×10⁻²⁷ kg, h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
items.ans:
p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 1.675×10⁻²⁷ × 0.025 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 3.66×10⁻²⁴ kg m/s; λ = h/p = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/3.66×10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.8×10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.18 nm. [1]
This wavelength is of the same order as the spacing between atoms in a crystal (about 0.1–0.3 nm), so the crystal acts like a diffraction grating for the neutron waves, and the diffraction pattern reveals the atomic arrangement. [1]

items.q: The depletion layer of a silicon p-n junction is 0.5 μm wide and the barrier potential is 0.7 V. (i) Estimate the average electric field in the depletion region. (ii) How would the width of the depletion layer change if both the p- and n-regions were doped more heavily? Give a reason.
items.ans:
(i) E ≈ V₀/d = 0.7/(0.5×10⁻⁶) = 1.4×10⁶ V/m, directed from the n-side to the p-side. [1]
(ii) It becomes narrower. With more donor and acceptor ions per unit volume, the charge needed to set up the barrier is uncovered within a smaller distance on each side of the junction. [1]

items.q: A charge of 2 μC is moved in a uniform electric field of 500 V/m from point A to point B. It first moves 0.4 m along the direction of the field and then 0.3 m perpendicular to the field. Find (i) the work done by the electric field on the charge, (ii) the potential difference V_A − V_B.
items.ans:
(i) Work is done by the field only during the displacement along the field; on the perpendicular part the force is normal to the displacement. W = qEd = 2×10⁻⁶ × 500 × 0.4 = 4×10⁻⁴ J. [1]
(ii) V_A − V_B = W/q = Ed = 500 × 0.4 = 200 V (A is at the higher potential; the 0.3 m perpendicular part lies along an equipotential). [1]

items.q: In a simple model of an excited hydrogen atom, the electron revolves in a circular orbit of radius 2.12×10⁻¹⁰ m, making 8.2×10¹⁴ revolutions per second. Find (i) the equivalent current, (ii) the magnetic field produced at the centre of the orbit. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
items.ans:
(i) Charge e passes any point of the orbit f times per second: I = ef = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 8.2×10¹⁴ ≈ 1.31×10⁻⁴ A. [1]
(ii) B = μ₀I/(2r) = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1.31×10⁻⁴/(2 × 2.12×10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 0.39 T. [1]

items.q: A ray of light is incident from air on the plane surface of a transparent medium at an angle of incidence of 60°, and the angle of refraction is found to be half the angle of incidence. Find (i) the refractive index of the medium, (ii) the critical angle for the medium–air interface.

The radius of a nucleus of mass number A is R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ = 1.2 fm. (i) Find the ratio of the radii of the nuclei ⁶⁴Cu and ⁸Be, and the radius of ⁶⁴Cu. (ii) Find the ratio of their volumes. What does this tell us about the density of nuclear matter in the two nuclei?
items.ans:
(i) R(Cu)/R(Be) = (64/8)^(1/3) = 8^(1/3) = 2. R(⁶⁴Cu) = 1.2 × 64^(1/3) = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 fm. [1]
(ii) Volume ∝ R³, so V(Cu)/V(Be) = 2³ = 8 = 64/8, the ratio of their mass numbers. Mass and volume are both proportional to A, so the density of nuclear matter is the same in both nuclei (independent of A). [1]

items.q: When a silicon diode is reverse biased, the small reverse current (a few μA) stays almost the same as the reverse voltage is increased from 1 V to 20 V, but it increases noticeably when the diode is warmed. Explain both observations.
items.ans:
The reverse current is due to minority carriers (electrons on the p-side, holes on the n-side) that drift across the junction. Even a small reverse voltage sweeps across every minority carrier that reaches the junction, so increasing the voltage cannot increase the current further — it 'saturates' (below breakdown). [1]
The number of minority carriers is fixed by thermal generation of electron–hole pairs, not by the applied voltage. Heating breaks more covalent bonds, generating more minority carriers, so the reverse current rises with temperature. [1]

items.q: (i) Compare electrical conductivity of metals, insulators and semiconductors based on band theory. (ii) Explain why diamond is insulator but tin is conductor though both are Group 14.
items.ans:
Metals: Overlapping/partially filled conduction band → free electrons → high conductivity.
Insulators: Large band gap (>5 eV) → negligible thermal excitation → poor conductivity.
Semiconductors: Moderate band gap (~1 eV) → some carriers at room temp → intermediate conductivity.
Diamond: Very large band gap (~5.4 eV) → insulator. Tin: Metallic bonding, overlapping bands → conductor.

items.q: Internal resistance of a car battery decreases as its temperature rises. Explain: (i) why the car starts more easily on a warm day, (ii) why the headlights dim momentarily when the starter motor is switched on, (iii) why the temperature of a heater element becomes constant after some time.
items.ans:
(i) Warm day: lower internal resistance r → larger current I = E/(R + r) for the starter → engine starts easily. [1]
(ii) The starter draws a very large current, so the drop Ir inside the battery is large and the terminal voltage V = E − Ir falls → headlights get less voltage and dim. [1]
(iii) At steady state, rate of heat production (I²R) = rate of heat loss to surroundings → temperature stays constant. [1]

items.q: Calculate binding energy and binding energy per nucleon for oxygen-16. (m_p=1.00727u, m_n=1.00866u, m_O=15.99493u, 1u=931.5 MeV)
Find critical angle for diamond (μ=2.42). A ray hits a face at 30°. Will it undergo total internal reflection? Also explain why diamond sparkles.
items.ans:
θ_c = sin⁻¹(1/2.42) = sin⁻¹(0.413) ≈ 24.4°.
Incident angle 30° is greater than θ_c → total internal reflection occurs.
Diamond is cut so that light undergoes multiple TIR inside before emerging — this causes its sparkle.

items.q: State Huygens' principle. Use it to derive Snell's law of refraction.
items.ans:
Huygens' Principle: Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; new wavefront is tangent to these wavelets.
Derivation: Let AB hit boundary. A reaches medium 2, point B still in medium 1. In time t: B→C (v₁t), A→E (v₂t). Refracted wavefront CE.
sin i = BC/AC = v₁t/AC; sin r = AE/AC = v₂t/AC.
sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁ → n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r (Snell's Law).

items.q: An ammeter reads up to 750 mA; galvanometer has Ig=100 mA, G=13 Ω. (i) Find shunt resistance. (ii) Why is the frame of a galvanometer made of metal?
items.ans:
(i) S = IgG/(I−Ig) = 100×13/(750−100) = 1300/650 = 2 Ω.
(ii) Metal frame provides electromagnetic damping — eddy currents in frame oppose coil oscillation → quick settling.

items.q: A solenoid: N turns, area A, length l. Find (i) Inductance L. If N→5N, A→25A, l→5l, find new inductance.

Using Gauss's law, obtain an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ. Hence find the field at a distance of 2 cm from a long wire with λ = 3 μC/m.
items.ans:
Take a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l. By symmetry E is radial and has the same magnitude on the curved surface; flux through the flat ends is zero. [1]
Φ = E(2πrl) = q_enc/ε₀ = λl/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r), directed radially outward for λ positive. [1]
E = 2kλ/r = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 3×10⁻⁶)/0.02 = 2.7×10⁶ N/C. [1]

items.q: When a cell is connected across a 4 Ω resistor the current is 0.5 A; when connected across a 9 Ω resistor the current is 0.25 A. Find (i) the emf and (ii) the internal resistance of the cell. (iii) What is the maximum current the cell can supply?

A metal rod PQ of length 0.5 m slides at a constant speed of 4 m/s on two parallel conducting rails, perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The total resistance of the circuit is 2 Ω. Find (i) the induced emf, (ii) the induced current, (iii) the force required to keep the rod moving at constant speed and the power delivered.
items.ans:
(i) e = Blv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.4 V. [1]
(ii) I = e/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A. [1]
(iii) Magnetic force opposing motion F = BIl = 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.02 N, so an equal external force 0.02 N is needed. Power = Fv = 0.02 × 4 = 0.08 W (= I²R = 0.04 × 2). [1]

items.q: A series LCR circuit has L = 0.4 H, C = 25 μF and R = 40 Ω and is connected to a 200 V (rms) source of variable frequency. Find (i) the resonant angular frequency, (ii) the rms current at resonance, (iii) the quality factor of the circuit.

A ray of light passes through an equilateral glass prism such that the angle of minimum deviation is 30°. Find (i) the refractive index of the glass, (ii) the angle of incidence. (iii) How does the ray travel inside the prism in this position?
items.ans:
(i) μ = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2) = sin 45°/sin 30° = 0.707/0.5 ≈ 1.414 (= √2). [1]
(ii) At minimum deviation i = e = (A + δ_m)/2 = (60° + 30°)/2 = 45°. [1]
(iii) The refracted ray inside travels parallel to the base of the prism (r₁ = r₂ = A/2 = 30°). [1]

items.q: In a hydrogen atom the energy of the electron in the nth orbit is E_n = −13.6/n² eV. (i) Find the wavelength of the photon emitted in the transition n = 3 → n = 2. (ii) Name the spectral series and region it belongs to. (iii) Find the ratio of radii of the 3rd and 2nd orbits.
items.ans:
(i) ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/9) = 13.6 × 5/36 ≈ 1.89 eV. λ = hc/ΔE = 1240 eV nm/1.89 eV ≈ 656 nm. [1]
(ii) Balmer series (final level n = 2); visible region (red line, Hα). [1]
(iii) r ∝ n² → r₃ : r₂ = 9 : 4. [1]

items.q: Calculate the energy released in the fusion reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n. Masses: ²H = 2.014102 u, ³H = 3.016049 u, ⁴He = 4.002603 u, n = 1.008665 u (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²). Why does such a reaction need a temperature of about 10⁷ K?
items.ans:
Mass of reactants = 2.014102 + 3.016049 = 5.030151 u; products = 4.002603 + 1.008665 = 5.011268 u. [1]
Δm = 0.018883 u → Q = 0.018883 × 931.5 ≈ 17.6 MeV released. [1]
Both nuclei are positively charged; they must have very large kinetic energy to overcome the Coulomb repulsion and come within range of the short-range nuclear force — such energies need temperatures ~10⁷ K. [1]

items.q: Charges of +2 μC, +2 μC and −4 μC are placed at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm. Find (i) the electrostatic potential energy of the system, (ii) the work needed to separate the charges to infinity, (iii) the potential at the centroid of the triangle.
items.ans:
(i) U = k(q₁q₂ + q₂q₃ + q₃q₁)/a = 9×10⁹ × (4 − 8 − 8)×10⁻¹²/0.1 = −1.08 J. [1]
(ii) Work needed = 0 − U = +1.08 J. [1]
(iii) All charges are at the same distance r = a/√3 from the centroid: V = k(2 + 2 − 4)×10⁻⁶/r = 0. [1]

items.q: Two cells, E₁ = 6 V (internal resistance 1 Ω) and E₂ = 4 V (internal resistance 2 Ω), are connected in parallel with their positive terminals joined, and this combination is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. Using Kirchhoff's rules, find the current through each cell and through the resistor.
items.ans:
Let V be the potential of the common positive terminal. Junction rule: (6 − V)/1 + (4 − V)/2 = V/4. [1]
24 − 4V + 8 − 2V = V → V = 32/7 ≈ 4.57 V. [1]
I₁ = (6 − 4.57)/1 ≈ 1.43 A (10/7 A, discharging); I₂ = (4 − 4.57)/2 ≈ −0.29 A, i.e. 0.29 A (2/7 A) flows INTO E₂ (it is being charged); I_R = 4.57/4 ≈ 1.14 A (8/7 A). [1]

items.q: A proton moving at 4×10⁵ m/s enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.05 T at an angle of 60° to the field. Describe its path and find (i) the radius of the path, (ii) the pitch. (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)
items.ans:
The velocity component along B (v cos 60°) is unaffected, while the perpendicular component (v sin 60°) gives circular motion → the path is a helix. [1]
(i) r = m v sin θ/(eB) = (1.67×10⁻²⁷ × 4×10⁵ × 0.866)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.05) ≈ 7.2×10⁻² m = 7.2 cm. [1]
(ii) T = 2πm/(eB) ≈ 1.31×10⁻⁶ s; pitch = v cos θ × T = 2×10⁵ × 1.31×10⁻⁶ ≈ 0.26 m. [1]

items.q: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries a current of 2 A. Its core is filled with a material of relative permeability 400. Find (i) the magnetic intensity H, (ii) the magnetic field B in the core, (iii) the magnetisation M of the core.

In Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 480 nm, the fringe width in air is 2.4 mm when the screen is 1.2 m from the slits. (i) Find the slit separation and the angular fringe width. (ii) Find the fringe width if the whole apparatus is immersed in water (μ = 4/3). (iii) What will be seen if one slit is covered?
items.ans:
(i) d = λD/β = (480×10⁻⁹ × 1.2)/(2.4×10⁻³) = 2.4×10⁻⁴ m = 0.24 mm; angular width θ = λ/d = β/D = 2×10⁻³ rad. [1]
(ii) In water λ' = λ/μ, so β' = β/μ = 2.4 × 3/4 = 1.8 mm. [1]
(iii) The interference fringes disappear; only the diffraction pattern of a single slit (broad bright centre with fainter bands) is seen. [1]

items.q: (i) Sketch the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number and state its main features. (ii) A nucleus of mass number 240 (BE per nucleon 7.6 MeV) splits into two nuclei of mass number 120 each (BE per nucleon 8.5 MeV). Find the energy released.
items.ans:
(i) BE/A rises steeply for light nuclei, reaches a broad maximum ≈ 8.75 MeV near A ≈ 56 (Fe), and decreases slowly to ≈ 7.6 MeV for A ≈ 240. Nearly constant BE/A for 30 ≤ A ≤ 170 shows the short-range, saturating nature of nuclear force. [1]
Heavy nuclei gain BE/A by splitting (fission); light nuclei by combining (fusion) — energy is released in both. [1]
(ii) Energy released = BE(products) − BE(parent) = 240 × 8.5 − 240 × 7.6 = 240 × 0.9 = 216 MeV. [1]

items.q: When light of wavelength 300 nm falls on a metal surface, the stopping potential is 1.85 V; for light of wavelength 400 nm it is 0.82 V. From these data find (i) Planck's constant, (ii) the work function of the metal. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, c = 3×10⁸ m/s)
items.ans:
Einstein's equation: eV₀ = hc/λ − φ₀. Subtracting for the two wavelengths: e(V₁ − V₂) = hc(1/λ₁ − 1/λ₂). [1]
(i) h = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.03/[3×10⁸ × (1/300 − 1/400)×10⁹] = 1.648×10⁻¹⁹/(3×10⁸ × 8.33×10⁵) ≈ 6.6×10⁻³⁴ J s. [1]
(ii) φ₀ = hc/λ₁ − eV₁ = (6.6×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸/3×10⁻⁷) J − 1.85 eV ≈ 4.13 eV − 1.85 eV ≈ 2.28 eV. [1]

items.q: Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are joined in series, and this combination is connected in parallel with a 4 μF capacitor. The arrangement is charged by a 10 V battery. Find (i) the equivalent capacitance, (ii) the charge on each capacitor and the potential difference across the 3 μF capacitor, (iii) the total energy stored.
items.ans:
(i) Series part: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 → 2 μF. Equivalent C = 2 + 4 = 6 μF. [1]
(ii) 4 μF: Q = 4 × 10 = 40 μC. Series branch: Q = 2 × 10 = 20 μC on each of the 3 μF and 6 μF. V across 3 μF = 20/3 ≈ 6.67 V (and 3.33 V across 6 μF). [1]
(iii) U = ½CV² = ½ × 6×10⁻⁶ × 10² = 3×10⁻⁴ J = 300 μJ. [1]

items.q: The tungsten filament of a 100 W, 220 V bulb has a resistance of 40 Ω at room temperature (20 °C). The temperature coefficient of resistance of tungsten is 4.5×10⁻³ °C⁻¹ (assume it constant). Find (i) the resistance of the filament when the bulb glows normally, (ii) the temperature of the filament, (iii) explain why bulbs usually fuse at the moment they are switched on.
items.ans:
(i) Hot resistance R = V²/P = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. [1]
(ii) R = R₀[1 + α(T − 20)] → 484 = 40[1 + 4.5×10⁻³(T − 20)] → T − 20 = 11.1/4.5×10⁻³ ≈ 2467 → T ≈ 2487 °C (about 2490 °C). [1]
(iii) When cold, the resistance is only 40 Ω, so the initial current 220/40 = 5.5 A is about 12 times the normal current (0.45 A). This sudden surge heats weak spots in the filament and can snap it. [1]

items.q: A rectangular coil of 20 turns, 8 cm × 5 cm, carries a current of 2 A in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. Find (i) the torque on the coil, (ii) the maximum torque possible. (iii) In which orientation is the coil in stable equilibrium?
items.ans:
Area A = 0.08 × 0.05 = 4×10⁻³ m²; the normal to the coil makes 60° with B. [½]
(i) τ = NIAB sin 60° = 20 × 2 × 4×10⁻³ × 0.5 × 0.866 ≈ 6.9×10⁻² N m. [1]
(ii) τ_max = NIAB = 0.08 N m (when the plane of the coil is parallel to B). [½]
(iii) Stable equilibrium when the magnetic moment (normal to the coil) is parallel to B, i.e. the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field; torque is then zero and potential energy minimum. [1]

items.q: A bulb rated 60 W, 120 V is to be operated from 240 V, 50 Hz mains by connecting a pure inductor in series with it. Find (i) the current through the bulb when it glows normally, (ii) the inductance required. (iii) Why is an inductor preferred to a resistor for this purpose?
items.ans:
(i) R = V²/P = 120²/60 = 240 Ω; I = P/V = 60/120 = 0.5 A. [1]
(ii) Z = 240/0.5 = 480 Ω; X_L = √(Z² − R²) = √(480² − 240²) ≈ 415.7 Ω; L = X_L/(2πf) = 415.7/(2π × 50) ≈ 1.32 H. [1]
(iii) A pure inductor consumes no average power (current and voltage across it differ in phase by 90°), whereas a series resistor would waste 0.5 × 120 = 60 W as heat. [1]

items.q: An object and a screen are fixed 90 cm apart. A convex lens placed between them gives a sharp image on the screen for two positions of the lens that are 30 cm apart. Find (i) the object distances for the two positions, (ii) the focal length of the lens, (iii) the ratio of the sizes of the two images.
items.ans:
(i) By symmetry the two positions interchange u and v: |u| + |v| = 90 and |v| − |u| = 30 → |u| = 30 cm, |v| = 60 cm for one position, and |u| = 60 cm, |v| = 30 cm for the other. [1]
(ii) 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/60 + 1/30 = 1/20 → f = 20 cm [or f = (D² − d²)/4D = (8100 − 900)/360 = 20 cm]. [1]
(iii) Magnifications are 60/30 = 2 and 30/60 = 0.5, so the image sizes are in the ratio 4 : 1 (both real, inverted). [1]

items.q: In a Geiger–Marsden experiment, an α-particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV moves head-on towards a gold nucleus (Z = 79). (i) Find its distance of closest approach. (ii) What is the impact parameter and the scattering angle in this case? (iii) What does this distance tell us about the size of the nucleus?
items.ans:
(i) At closest approach K = k(2e)(Ze)/r₀ → r₀ = (9×10⁹ × 2 × 79 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(5 × 1.6×10⁻¹³) ≈ 4.6×10⁻¹⁴ m (≈ 46 fm). [1]
(ii) Head-on: impact parameter b = 0; the α-particle retraces its path, scattering angle 180°. [1]
(iii) The nucleus must be smaller than about 4.6×10⁻¹⁴ m — this gives an upper limit to nuclear size, about 10⁻⁴ of the atomic size (10⁻¹⁰ m). [1]

items.q: A laser pointer emits 5 mW of light of wavelength 663 nm. Find (i) the energy of each photon in eV, (ii) the number of photons emitted per second. (iii) Will this light eject photoelectrons from caesium (work function 2.14 eV)? Would a more powerful laser of the same wavelength help? (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s)
items.ans:
(i) E = hc/λ = (6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸)/(663×10⁻⁹) = 3.0×10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 1.88 eV. [1]
(ii) N = P/E = 5×10⁻³/3.0×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.7×10¹⁶ photons per second. [1]
(iii) No — 1.88 eV is less than 2.14 eV. A more powerful laser only gives more photons of the same energy, and each electron absorbs one photon, so still no emission. [1]

items.q: (i) Using Gauss's law, obtain the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet with uniform surface charge density σ. (ii) Two large, thin parallel metal plates carry surface charge densities +17.7 nC/m² and −17.7 nC/m² on their inner faces. Find the electric field in the region between them and outside them. (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
items.ans:
(i) Take a cylindrical Gaussian surface of cross-section A piercing the sheet; E is perpendicular to the sheet, so flux passes only through the two flat ends: Φ = 2EA. Enclosed charge = σA. 2EA = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀), directed away from the sheet for σ positive. [1½]
(ii) Between the plates the fields of the two sheets add: E = σ/ε₀ = 17.7×10⁻⁹/8.85×10⁻¹² = 2×10³ N/C, from the positive to the negative plate. [1]
Outside, the two fields are equal and opposite → E = 0. [½]

items.q: Six identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series to an external resistance of 6 Ω. Find (i) the current in the circuit, (ii) the potential difference across the external resistance. (iii) Find the current if one of the cells is connected the wrong way round by mistake.
items.ans:
(i) Total emf = 6 × 1.5 = 9 V; total internal resistance = 6 × 0.5 = 3 Ω. I = 9/(6 + 3) = 1 A. [1]
(ii) V = IR = 1 × 6 = 6 V. [1]
(iii) The reversed cell opposes: net emf = 5 × 1.5 − 1.5 = 6 V, but internal resistance is still 3 Ω. I = 6/9 ≈ 0.67 A. [1]

items.q: A wire carrying a current of 4 A is bent into a semicircular arc of radius 5 cm. The current is led in and out of the arc by two long straight wires that lie along the radial lines through the two ends of the arc (extending outward, away from the centre). Find the magnetic field at the centre of the arc. Why do the straight portions contribute nothing? State the direction of the field.
items.ans:
Biot–Savart: each element of the arc is perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre, so B_arc = (μ₀I/4πR) × πR/R = μ₀I/(4R). [1]
B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 4)/(4 × 0.05) ≈ 2.5×10⁻⁵ T. [1]
The straight parts lie along lines through the centre, so dl × r = 0 for them and they contribute no field. Direction: perpendicular to the plane of the arc, given by the right-hand rule (out of the page for anticlockwise current as seen by the viewer). [1]

items.q: A step-down transformer at a village substation is not 100% efficient. Name three causes of energy loss in a real transformer and state how each is reduced in practice.
items.ans:
(1) Copper (joule) loss: heating I²R in the windings — reduced by using thick copper wire for the high-current winding. [1]
(2) Eddy-current loss: currents induced in the iron core heat it — reduced by using a laminated core (thin insulated sheets). [1]
(3) Flux leakage: not all primary flux links the secondary — reduced by winding the primary and secondary one over the other on a closed (shell-type) core. (Also acceptable: hysteresis loss in the core, reduced by using soft iron with a narrow loop; humming/vibration losses.) [1]

items.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 0.3 mm apart and the screen is 1.2 m away. The slits are illuminated by light containing two wavelengths, 600 nm and 480 nm. Find (i) the distance of the third bright fringe of the 600 nm light from the central maximum, (ii) the least distance from the central maximum at which bright fringes of both wavelengths coincide, (iii) the ratio of the fringe widths of the two patterns.

When lithium-7 is bombarded with protons, the reaction ⁷₃Li + ¹₁H → ⁴₂He + ⁴₂He takes place. (i) Show that charge and the number of nucleons are conserved. (ii) Find the energy released (Q-value). (iii) In what form does this energy mainly appear? Masses: ⁷Li = 7.016004 u, ¹H = 1.007825 u, ⁴He = 4.002603 u; 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².
items.ans:
(i) Charge: 3 + 1 = 2 + 2 = 4; nucleons: 7 + 1 = 4 + 4 = 8 — both conserved. [1]
(ii) Δm = (7.016004 + 1.007825) − 2 × 4.002603 = 8.023829 − 8.005206 = 0.018623 u; Q = 0.018623 × 931.5 ≈ 17.3 MeV. [1]
(iii) Mainly as kinetic energy of the two α-particles, which fly apart (the energy comes from the increase in total binding energy). [1]

items.q: Explain, with a labelled circuit diagram, how a p-n junction diode works as a half-wave rectifier. Draw (describe) the input and output waveforms. Why is a full-wave rectifier usually preferred, and what is the output frequency of each for a 50 Hz input?
items.ans:
Circuit: AC from the secondary of a transformer is applied to a diode in series with a load resistor R_L; output taken across R_L. [1]
During the positive half-cycle the diode is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through R_L; during the negative half-cycle it is reverse biased and practically no current flows. Output: positive half-sine pulses with gaps (pulsating DC). [1]
A full-wave rectifier uses both half-cycles, giving higher average output and easier smoothing. Output (ripple) frequency: half-wave 50 Hz, full-wave 100 Hz. [1]

items.q: A 10 pF parallel plate air capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. A slab of dielectric constant 5 is now inserted to fill the space between the plates completely. Find (i) the new capacitance and potential difference, (ii) the energy stored before and after inserting the slab. (iii) Account for the change in energy.
items.ans:
(i) Charge stays the same, Q = C₀V₀ = 10×10⁻¹² × 100 = 1×10⁻⁹ C. C = KC₀ = 50 pF; V = Q/C = 100/5 = 20 V. [1]
(ii) U₀ = ½C₀V₀² = ½ × 10×10⁻¹² × 100² = 5×10⁻⁸ J; U = ½CV² = ½ × 50×10⁻¹² × 20² = 1×10⁻⁸ J (= U₀/K). [1]
(iii) Energy decreases by 4×10⁻⁸ J. The field pulls the slab into the capacitor (the induced charges on the slab are attracted by the plates); this energy is the work done by the field on the slab (it becomes kinetic energy/heat, or work done on the agent holding the slab back). [1]

items.q: A battery of emf 9 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a network in which a 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are joined in parallel, and this combination is in series with a 2 Ω resistor. Find (i) the current drawn from the battery, (ii) the terminal potential difference of the battery, (iii) the current through the 6 Ω and the 3 Ω resistors.

A long straight solid cylindrical wire of radius a carries a steady current I distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Using Ampere's circuital law, find the magnetic field (i) at a distance r less than a from the axis, (ii) at a distance r greater than a. (iii) For a = 2 mm and I = 10 A, find the field at r = 1 mm and at r = 4 mm.
items.ans:
Take a circular Amperian loop of radius r coaxial with the wire; B is tangential and of constant magnitude on it, so ∮B·dl = B(2πr). [½]
(i) r less than a: current enclosed = I(πr²/πa²) = Ir²/a² → B(2πr) = μ₀Ir²/a² → B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²) (B ∝ r). [1]
(ii) r greater than a: enclosed current = I → B = μ₀I/(2πr) (B ∝ 1/r). [½]
(iii) r = 1 mm: B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 10 × 1×10⁻³)/(2π × (2×10⁻³)²) = 5×10⁻⁴ T. r = 4 mm: B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 4×10⁻³) = 5×10⁻⁴ T (the same value, since the field is maximum at r = a and falls on both sides). [1]

items.q: A 100 Ω resistor and a capacitor are connected in series across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms voltage across the resistor is found to be 110 V. Find (i) the rms current, (ii) the rms voltage across the capacitor, (iii) the capacitance. Why is the sum of the two voltmeter readings greater than 220 V?
items.ans:
(i) I = V_R/R = 110/100 = 1.1 A. [½]
(ii) V_R and V_C are 90° out of phase: V² = V_R² + V_C² → V_C = √(220² − 110²) ≈ 190.5 V. [1]
(iii) X_C = V_C/I = 190.5/1.1 ≈ 173.2 Ω; C = 1/(2πfX_C) = 1/(2π × 50 × 173.2) ≈ 1.84×10⁻⁵ F ≈ 18.4 μF. [1]
The voltages are not in phase, so they add as phasors (vectors), not arithmetically; 110 + 190.5 is greater than 220, but √(110² + 190.5²) = 220 V. [½]

items.q: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm and a concave lens of focal length 10 cm are placed coaxially 30 cm apart. An object is placed 30 cm in front of the convex lens (on the side away from the concave lens). Find (i) the position of the image formed by the convex lens, (ii) the position and nature of the final image, (iii) the total magnification.
items.ans:
(i) Convex lens: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 → v₁ = +60 cm (60 cm beyond the convex lens). [1]
(ii) This point is 60 − 30 = 30 cm beyond the concave lens, so it acts as a virtual object: u₂ = +30 cm, f₂ = −10 cm. 1/v = −1/10 + 1/30 = −1/15 → v₂ = −15 cm: the final image is virtual, 15 cm in front of the concave lens (i.e. between the two lenses, 15 cm from each). [1]
(iii) m₁ = v₁/u₁ = 60/(−30) = −2; m₂ = v₂/u₂ = −15/30 = −0.5; m = m₁m₂ = +1: the final image is erect and of the same size as the object. [1]

items.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of (i) a cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 40 m/s, (ii) an electron moving at the same speed of 40 m/s. (iii) Why do we never observe wave effects such as diffraction with a cricket ball? (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg)
items.ans:
(i) λ = h/(mv) = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(0.15 × 40) ≈ 1.1×10⁻³⁴ m. [1]
(ii) λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹ × 40) ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ m (about 18 μm). [1]
(iii) Wave effects are noticeable only when λ is comparable to the size of obstacles/apertures. 10⁻³⁴ m is far smaller than even a nucleus (10⁻¹⁵ m), so the ball's wave nature is undetectable; its motion is described by classical mechanics. [1]

items.q: A 5 V battery (negligible internal resistance) is connected through a 100 Ω resistor to two branches joined in parallel. Branch 1 has a silicon diode D₁ in series with a 50 Ω resistor, connected so that D₁ is forward biased; branch 2 has an identical diode D₂ in series with a 50 Ω resistor, connected so that D₂ is reverse biased. Each diode has a 0.7 V drop when conducting and infinite resistance in reverse. Find (i) the current drawn from the battery, (ii) the current in each branch. (iii) What changes if the battery terminals are interchanged?
items.ans:
(i) D₂ is reverse biased, so branch 2 carries no current. Circuit: 100 Ω + D₁ + 50 Ω in series. I = (5 − 0.7)/(100 + 50) = 4.3/150 ≈ 0.0287 A ≈ 28.7 mA. [1]
(ii) Branch 1 (D₁): 28.7 mA; branch 2 (D₂): zero. [1]
(iii) D₁ becomes reverse biased and D₂ forward biased; the same current, 28.7 mA, now flows through branch 2 (in the opposite direction) and branch 1 carries none. [1]

items.q: Point charges +1 μC, +1 μC and −1 μC are placed at the corners A, B and C respectively of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm in air. Find (i) the magnitude and direction of the net force on the charge at C, (ii) the net electric field at the midpoint M of AB due to all three charges.
items.ans:
(i) Each of A and B attracts C with F = kq²/a² = 9×10⁹ × (10⁻⁶)²/(0.1)² = 0.9 N, along CA and CB, which are 60° apart. [1]
Resultant = 2F cos 30° = 2 × 0.9 × 0.866 ≈ 1.56 N, along the bisector of angle C, i.e. from C towards the midpoint of AB. [1]
(ii) At M the fields of the equal charges at A and B are equal and opposite and cancel. Distance CM = a√3/2 ≈ 0.0866 m, so E = kq/CM² = 9×10⁹ × 10⁻⁶/0.0075 = 1.2×10⁶ N/C, directed from M towards C (towards the negative charge). [1]

items.q: A uniform wire 1 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 2 Ω. (i) Find the resistivity of its material. (ii) The wire is bent into a circle. Find the resistance between two diametrically opposite points. (iii) Find the resistance between two points that are a quarter of the circumference apart.
items.ans:
(i) ρ = RA/l = 2 × 0.5×10⁻⁶/1 = 1×10⁻⁶ Ω m. [1]
(ii) The two halves (1 Ω each) are in parallel: R = 1 × 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5 Ω. [1]
(iii) Arcs of ¼ and ¾ of the wire: 0.5 Ω and 1.5 Ω in parallel: R = 0.5 × 1.5/2.0 = 0.375 Ω. [1]

items.q: Two circular loops of radii 10 cm and 20 cm lie in the same plane and have a common centre O. They carry currents of 2 A and 3 A respectively. Find the magnetic field at O when the currents are (i) in the same sense, (ii) in opposite senses. (iii) State the direction of the field in case (i).
items.ans:
B₁ = μ₀I₁/(2r₁) = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 2)/(2 × 0.10) ≈ 1.26×10⁻⁵ T; B₂ = μ₀I₂/(2r₂) = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 3)/(2 × 0.20) ≈ 0.94×10⁻⁵ T. [1]
(i) Same sense: B = B₁ + B₂ ≈ 2.2×10⁻⁵ T. (ii) Opposite senses: B = B₁ − B₂ ≈ 3.1×10⁻⁶ T, in the direction of the field of the inner loop. [1]
(iii) Perpendicular to the plane of the loops: out of the page if the currents are anticlockwise as seen by the viewer, into the page if clockwise (right-hand thumb rule). [1]

items.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.01 m² is held with its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field, which decreases uniformly from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.2 s. The coil is connected to a circuit of total resistance 4 Ω. Find (i) the induced emf, (ii) the induced current, (iii) the total charge that flows. Explain how Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of energy.
items.ans:
(i) |e| = N A ΔB/Δt = 200 × 0.01 × (0.5 − 0.1)/0.2 = 4 V. [1]
(ii) I = e/R = 4/4 = 1 A; (iii) q = NΔφ/R = 200 × 0.01 × 0.4/4 = 0.2 C (= I × t = 1 × 0.2). [1]
If the induced current aided the change of flux, it would increase the change further, producing ever larger current and energy from nothing. Since the induced current opposes the change, work must be done (or field energy used) to create it — energy is conserved. [1]

items.q: A glass sphere (μ = 1.5) of radius 10 cm has a small air bubble 4 cm from its centre. Find the apparent position of the bubble when it is viewed (i) from the side of the sphere nearer to the bubble, (ii) from the opposite side, looking along the diameter through the bubble. (iii) Why are the two apparent positions different?
items.ans:
Use μ₂/v − μ₁/u = (μ₂ − μ₁)/R with light going from glass (μ₁ = 1.5) to air (μ₂ = 1); the centre of the sphere lies on the incident side, so R = −10 cm. [½]
(i) Nearer side: u = −(10 − 4) = −6 cm. 1/v = −0.5/(−10) + 1.5/(−6) = 0.05 − 0.25 = −0.2 → v = −5 cm: the bubble appears 5 cm inside the surface (1 cm nearer than its real position). [1]
(ii) Far side: u = −(10 + 4) = −14 cm. 1/v = 0.05 − 1.5/14 = 0.05 − 0.107 = −0.057 → v ≈ −17.5 cm: it appears 17.5 cm inside the surface (3.5 cm farther than its real position). [1]
(iii) The bubble is at different distances (6 cm and 14 cm) from the two refracting points, and the centre of curvature is on the bubble's side in both cases; the curved surface shifts the image by an amount that depends on the object distance, so the two apparent positions differ. [½]

items.q: Using Bohr's postulates, derive an expression for the radius of the nth orbit of the electron in a hydrogen atom. Calculate the radius of the first orbit and of the third orbit. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
items.ans:
Electrostatic attraction provides the centripetal force: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²). Quantisation of angular momentum: mvr = nh/2π → v = nh/(2πmr). [1]
Substituting: m(nh/2πmr)²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²) → rₙ = ε₀n²h²/(πme²), i.e. r ∝ n². [1]
r₁ = (8.85×10⁻¹² × (6.63×10⁻³⁴)²)/(π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²) ≈ 5.3×10⁻¹¹ m = 0.53 Å; r₃ = 9r₁ ≈ 4.8×10⁻¹⁰ m ≈ 4.77 Å. [1]

items.q: Compare the energy released per kilogram of fuel in (i) the fission of U-235, given that each fission releases about 200 MeV, and (ii) the fusion reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n, which releases 17.6 MeV per reaction (take the mass of the reactants as 5.03 g per mole of reactions). (iii) Find the ratio of the two values. (N_A = 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹, 1 MeV = 1.602×10⁻¹³ J)
items.ans:
(i) Nuclei in 1 kg U-235 = (1000/235) × 6.022×10²³ ≈ 2.56×10²⁴; E = 2.56×10²⁴ × 200 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ ≈ 8.2×10¹³ J/kg. [1]
(ii) Reactions per kg of D–T fuel = (1000/5.03) × 6.022×10²³ ≈ 1.20×10²⁶; E = 1.20×10²⁶ × 17.6 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ ≈ 3.4×10¹⁴ J/kg. [1]
(iii) Ratio fusion : fission ≈ 3.4×10¹⁴/8.2×10¹³ ≈ 4.1 — fusion gives about four times more energy per kilogram of fuel (though less per reaction). [1]

items.q: Two isolated conducting spheres of radii 2 cm and 6 cm are far apart and are then connected by a thin conducting wire. A total charge of 80 nC is shared between them. Find (i) the charge on each sphere, (ii) their common potential, (iii) the ratio of the surface charge densities σ₁ : σ₂. Use this to explain why charge collects at the sharp points of a conductor. (k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
items.ans:
(i) Connected spheres reach the same potential: kq₁/r₁ = kq₂/r₂ → q₁/q₂ = r₁/r₂ = 2/6 = 1/3. With q₁ + q₂ = 80 nC: q₁ = 20 nC, q₂ = 60 nC. [1]
(ii) V = kq₁/r₁ = 9×10⁹ × 20×10⁻⁹/0.02 = 9000 V (same for the larger sphere: 9×10⁹ × 60×10⁻⁹/0.06 = 9000 V). [1]
(iii) σ = q/4πr², so σ₁/σ₂ = (q₁/q₂)(r₂/r₁)² = (1/3)(9) = 3 : 1, i.e. σ ∝ 1/r. A sharp point behaves like a sphere of very small radius, so the surface charge density (and the field) is greatest there. [1]

items.q: Two bulbs rated 100 W, 220 V and 60 W, 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Find (i) the resistance of each bulb, (ii) the power actually consumed by each bulb. (iii) Which bulb glows brighter in this arrangement, and which would glow brighter if they were joined in parallel across the same supply? (Assume the resistances stay constant.)
items.ans:
(i) R = V²/P: R₁ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω; R₂ = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω. [1]
(ii) I = 220/(484 + 807) ≈ 0.170 A. P₁ = I²R₁ ≈ 14.1 W; P₂ = I²R₂ ≈ 23.4 W. [1]
(iii) In series the current is the same, so the bulb of larger resistance (the 60 W bulb) dissipates more power and glows brighter. In parallel the voltage is the same, P = V²/R, so the 100 W bulb (smaller R) glows brighter. [1]

items.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. A rectangular loop with sides 10 cm and 5 cm lies in the same plane, with its 10 cm sides parallel to the wire; the nearer 10 cm side is 2 cm from the wire. The loop carries a current of 5 A, flowing in the nearer side in the same direction as the current in the wire. Find the net force on the loop and state its direction. Why do the 5 cm sides give no net force? (μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m/A)
items.ans:
Force on a side of length L at distance d: F = μ₀I₁I₂L/(2πd). Near side (d = 0.02 m, parallel currents): F₁ = 2×10⁻⁷ × 10 × 5 × 0.1/0.02 = 5.0×10⁻⁵ N, attractive. Far side (d = 0.07 m, antiparallel currents): F₂ = 2×10⁻⁷ × 10 × 5 × 0.1/0.07 ≈ 1.43×10⁻⁵ N, repulsive. [1]
Net force = 5.0×10⁻⁵ − 1.43×10⁻⁵ ≈ 3.6×10⁻⁵ N, directed towards the wire (attraction). [1]
The two 5 cm sides carry opposite currents at the same distances from the wire, so the forces on them are equal and opposite (along the wire's length direction) and cancel. [1]

items.q: A hydroelectric station in Himachal Pradesh sends 800 kW of electric power to a town through transmission lines of total resistance 5 Ω. Find the power lost as heat in the lines if the power is transmitted at (i) 4 kV, (ii) 40 kV. (iii) What fraction of the power is lost in each case, and what device makes high-voltage transmission possible?
items.ans:
(i) I = P/V = 800×10³/4000 = 200 A; loss = I²R = 200² × 5 = 2.0×10⁵ W = 200 kW. [1]
(ii) I = 800×10³/40 000 = 20 A; loss = 20² × 5 = 2000 W = 2 kW. [1]
(iii) Fraction lost: 200/800 = 25 % at 4 kV, but only 2/800 = 0.25 % at 40 kV (loss ∝ 1/V²). A step-up transformer raises the voltage at the station and step-down transformers lower it near the consumers. [1]

items.q: Students at a school in Shirdi build a solar concentrator using a concave mirror of focal length 1.0 m and aperture (diameter) 50 cm, pointed straight at the Sun. (i) Where is the image of the Sun formed, and why? (ii) The Sun subtends an angle of about 0.5° at the Earth. Find the diameter of the Sun's image. (iii) Assuming all the light falling on the mirror is reflected, by what factor is the intensity of sunlight increased at the image?
items.ans:
(i) The Sun is effectively at infinity, so the rays from any point on it arrive parallel and the image is formed in the focal plane, 1.0 m from the mirror (real, inverted, small). [1]
(ii) Rays from the two edges of the Sun arrive at angle θ = 0.5° = 8.73×10⁻³ rad to each other, so the image diameter d = fθ = 1.0 × 8.73×10⁻³ m ≈ 8.7 mm. [1]
(iii) The power collected over the mirror's area is concentrated into the image area: factor = (D/d)² = (0.50/8.73×10⁻³)² ≈ 3.3×10³. [1]

items.q: For the photoelectric effect, draw (describe) the graphs of photoelectric current against the potential of the collector (anode) relative to the emitter: (i) for two different intensities of light of the same frequency, (ii) for two different frequencies of light of the same intensity. (iii) Explain what each pair of graphs shows about the effect of intensity and frequency.
items.ans:
(i) Same frequency, intensities I₂ > I₁: both curves rise and level off at saturation currents, the higher intensity giving the larger saturation current; both cut the voltage axis at the same negative value −V₀ (same stopping potential). [1]
(ii) Same intensity, frequencies ν₂ > ν₁: both reach (about) the same saturation current, but the curve for ν₂ cuts the axis at a more negative voltage, i.e. a larger stopping potential. [1]
(iii) Intensity decides the number of photons, hence the number of photoelectrons (saturation current), but not their maximum energy. Frequency decides the energy of each photon, so eV₀ = K_max = hν − φ₀ increases with frequency. [1]

items.q: In a nuclear reactor, one possible fission of uranium-235 is ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n. Using the masses ²³⁵U = 235.043930 u, ¹⁴¹Ba = 140.914411 u, ⁹²Kr = 91.926156 u, n = 1.008665 u, find (i) the mass defect, (ii) the energy released per fission in MeV, (iii) the energy released (in kWh) by the complete fission of 1 g of U-235. (1 u = 931.5 MeV, N_A = 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹, 1 MeV = 1.602×10⁻¹³ J)

A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.03 m² separated by 3 mm. Find its capacitance when (i) the gap is filled with two slabs, each 1.5 mm thick, of dielectric constants 2 and 5, one on top of the other; (ii) the gap is filled with two slabs, each 3 mm thick and covering half the plate area, of dielectric constants 2 and 5 placed side by side. (iii) Which arrangement gives the larger capacitance? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
items.ans:
(i) Layers one above the other behave as capacitors in series: C = ε₀A/(t₁/K₁ + t₂/K₂) = (8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.03)/(0.0015/2 + 0.0015/5) = 2.655×10⁻¹³/(1.05×10⁻³) ≈ 2.53×10⁻¹⁰ F ≈ 253 pF. [1]
(ii) Side-by-side slabs behave as capacitors in parallel: C = ε₀(A/2)(K₁ + K₂)/d = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.015 × 7/0.003 ≈ 3.10×10⁻¹⁰ F ≈ 310 pF. [1]
(iii) The side-by-side (parallel) arrangement gives the larger capacitance, 310 pF > 253 pF. [1]

items.q: A potential difference of 0.2 V is applied across a copper wire 0.5 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1.0 mm². The density of free electrons in copper is 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ and the electron mobility is 4.3×10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Find (i) the drift speed of the electrons, (ii) the current in the wire, (iii) the average relaxation time of the electrons. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg)

A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 1 A. Find the magnetic field (i) at its centre, (ii) at a point on its axis 10 cm from the centre. (iii) At what distance from the centre, on the axis, is the field one-eighth of its value at the centre? (μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m/A)

A series circuit containing an inductor of 0.1 H, a capacitor of 50 μF and a resistor of 20 Ω is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (i) the inductive and capacitive reactances, (ii) the impedance and the rms current, (iii) the phase angle, stating whether the current leads or lags the voltage.
items.ans:
(i) X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω; X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 50×10⁻⁶) ≈ 63.7 Ω. [1]
(ii) Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] = √[20² + (−32.2)²] ≈ 37.9 Ω; I_rms = 220/37.9 ≈ 5.8 A. [1]
(iii) tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R = −32.2/20 → |φ| ≈ 58°. Since X_C > X_L the circuit is capacitive and the current leads the voltage by about 58° (power factor ≈ 0.53). [1]

items.q: A single slit is illuminated by monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm, and the diffraction pattern is seen on a screen 2 m away. The width of the central bright band is 4.8 mm. Find (i) the width of the slit, (ii) the angular position of the first minimum. (iii) What will the width of the central band be if light of wavelength 450 nm is used instead? What happens to it if the whole apparatus (with 600 nm light) is immersed in water of μ = 4/3?
items.ans:
(i) Width of central maximum = 2λD/a → a = 2λD/w = (2 × 600×10⁻⁹ × 2)/(4.8×10⁻³) = 5×10⁻⁴ m = 0.5 mm. [1]
(ii) First minimum at θ = λ/a = 600×10⁻⁹/5×10⁻⁴ = 1.2×10⁻³ rad (on either side of the centre). [1]
(iii) Width ∝ λ: w = 4.8 × 450/600 = 3.6 mm. In water the wavelength becomes 600/(4/3) = 450 nm, so the central band also narrows to 3.6 mm. [1]

items.q: (i) Using Bohr's model, show that the speed of the electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen is inversely proportional to n, and its frequency of revolution is inversely proportional to n³. (ii) The speed of the electron in the first orbit is 2.18×10⁶ m/s and the radius of that orbit is 0.53×10⁻¹⁰ m. Find the speed and the frequency of revolution of the electron in the third orbit.
items.ans:
(i) mvr = nh/2π and mv²/r = ke²/r². Dividing: v = 2πke²/(nh), so v ∝ 1/n; and r = n²h²/(4π²mke²), so r ∝ n². [1]
Frequency f = v/(2πr) ∝ (1/n)/n² = 1/n³. [1]
(ii) v₃ = v₁/3 = 2.18×10⁶/3 ≈ 7.3×10⁵ m/s. r₃ = 9r₁ = 4.77×10⁻¹⁰ m; f₃ = v₃/(2πr₃) = 7.27×10⁵/(2π × 4.77×10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 2.4×10¹⁴ Hz (= f₁/27, with f₁ ≈ 6.5×10¹⁵ Hz). [1]

items.q: Using the atomic masses ¹H = 1.007825 u, n = 1.008665 u, ²H = 2.014102 u and ⁴He = 4.002603 u, find (i) the binding energy per nucleon of the deuteron ²H, (ii) the binding energy per nucleon of ⁴He. (iii) Find the energy released when two deuterons fuse to form one ⁴He nucleus, and explain why energy is released. (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
items.ans:
(i) Δm(²H) = 1.007825 + 1.008665 − 2.014102 = 0.002388 u → BE = 0.002388 × 931.5 ≈ 2.22 MeV; per nucleon ≈ 1.11 MeV. [1]
(ii) Δm(⁴He) = 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) − 4.002603 = 0.030377 u → BE ≈ 28.3 MeV; per nucleon ≈ 7.07 MeV. [1]
(iii) Energy released = BE(⁴He) − 2 × BE(²H) = 28.30 − 4.45 ≈ 23.8 MeV. The product is far more tightly bound (7.07 MeV vs 1.11 MeV per nucleon); the increase in total binding energy appears as kinetic energy of the products. [1]

items.q: In a region of space the electric field is E = (500x) î N/C, where x is in metres. A cube of side 0.1 m is placed with its edges along the axes, with one face in the plane x = 0.1 m and the opposite face in the plane x = 0.2 m. Find (i) the electric flux through each of these two faces and through the other four faces, (ii) the net flux through the cube, (iii) the charge enclosed by the cube. (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
items.ans:
(i) Face at x = 0.1 m (outward normal −î): E = 50 N/C, Φ₁ = −50 × 0.01 = −0.5 N m² C⁻¹. Face at x = 0.2 m (normal +î): E = 100 N/C, Φ₂ = +100 × 0.01 = +1.0 N m² C⁻¹. The other four faces are parallel to E, so the flux through each is zero. [1]
(ii) Net flux Φ = −0.5 + 1.0 = 0.5 N m² C⁻¹. [1]
(iii) By Gauss's law q = ε₀Φ = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.5 ≈ 4.4×10⁻¹² C (positive). [1]

items.q: A uniform wire has a resistance of 12 Ω. (i) It is stretched uniformly to twice its original length. Find its new resistance. (ii) The stretched wire is cut into four equal pieces, which are joined in parallel. Find the resistance of the combination. (iii) This combination is connected across a cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. Find the current drawn from the cell and the terminal potential difference.
items.ans:
(i) The volume is unchanged, so doubling the length halves the area: R ∝ l/A ∝ l² → R' = 4 × 12 = 48 Ω. [1]
(ii) Each piece has 48/4 = 12 Ω; four 12 Ω pieces in parallel give 12/4 = 3 Ω. [1]
(iii) I = E/(R + r) = 6/(3 + 1) = 1.5 A; terminal p.d. V = E − Ir = 6 − 1.5 × 1 = 4.5 V. [1]

items.q: Two long straight parallel wires A and B are 12 cm apart in air and carry currents of 4 A and 8 A respectively, in the same direction. (i) Find the force per metre length between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. (ii) Where, between the wires, should a third long parallel wire carrying a current be placed so that it experiences no net force? (iii) Does this position depend on the magnitude or the direction of the current in the third wire? (μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
items.ans:
(i) F/l = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2×10⁻⁷ × 4 × 8/0.12 ≈ 5.3×10⁻⁵ N/m; currents in the same direction attract. [1]
(ii) The net field must be zero there: μ₀(4)/(2πx) = μ₀(8)/(2π(0.12 − x)) → 4(0.12 − x) = 8x → x = 0.04 m. The third wire must be 4 cm from A (8 cm from B), in the plane of the wires. [1]
(iii) No. At that point the field of A and B is zero, so the force I₃lB on the third wire is zero for any current, whatever its magnitude or direction. [1]

items.q: A pure inductor of 0.5 H and a resistor of 100 Ω are connected in series with a capacitor C across a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. (i) Find the value of C for which the power factor of the circuit is unity. (ii) Find the rms current in this condition. (iii) Find the rms voltage across the inductor, and explain how it can be larger than the supply voltage.
items.ans:
(i) Unity power factor means resonance: X_L = X_C → C = 1/(ω²L) = 1/((100π)² × 0.5) ≈ 2.03×10⁻⁵ F ≈ 20.3 μF. [1]
(ii) At resonance Z = R, so I = V/R = 230/100 = 2.3 A. [1]
(iii) X_L = ωL = 100π × 0.5 ≈ 157 Ω; V_L = IX_L = 2.3 × 157 ≈ 361 V. The voltage across C is also 361 V but exactly opposite in phase (180° apart), so V_L and V_C cancel; the supply only has to provide the voltage across R (230 V). The individual voltages are not limited by the supply voltage. [1]

items.q: An object is placed 30 cm to the left of a convex lens L₁ of focal length 20 cm. A second convex lens L₂ of focal length 10 cm is placed coaxially 80 cm to the right of L₁. Find (i) the position of the image formed by L₁, (ii) the position of the final image, (iii) the total magnification, and state the nature of the final image.
items.ans:
(i) For L₁: 1/v₁ = 1/f₁ + 1/u₁ = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 → v₁ = +60 cm (real image 60 cm to the right of L₁). [1]
(ii) This image is 80 − 60 = 20 cm to the left of L₂, so u₂ = −20 cm: 1/v₂ = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20 → v₂ = +20 cm, i.e. 20 cm to the right of L₂. [1]
(iii) m₁ = v₁/u₁ = 60/(−30) = −2; m₂ = v₂/u₂ = 20/(−20) = −1; m = m₁m₂ = +2. The final image is real, erect (relative to the object) and twice the size of the object. [1]

items.q: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the radius of the nth orbit is r_n = 0.53n² Å and the speed of the electron in it is v_n = (2.19×10⁶/n) m/s. (i) Find the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the n = 2 orbit. (ii) Show that the circumference of this orbit contains exactly two such wavelengths. (iii) Explain how de Broglie's idea accounts for Bohr's quantisation condition. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg)
items.ans:
(i) v₂ = 1.095×10⁶ m/s; λ = h/(mv₂) = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹ × 1.095×10⁶) ≈ 6.65×10⁻¹⁰ m = 6.65 Å. [1]
(ii) r₂ = 0.53 × 4 = 2.12 Å; circumference 2πr₂ = 2π × 2.12 ≈ 13.3 Å = 2 × 6.65 Å. [1]
(iii) The electron wave in a stationary orbit must form a standing wave, so the circumference must hold a whole number of wavelengths: 2πr_n = nλ = nh/(mv). Rearranged, mv r_n = nh/2π, which is Bohr's condition for quantisation of angular momentum. [1]

items.q: The Sun's energy comes from fusion in its core, in which, overall, four hydrogen atoms are converted into one helium atom (the positrons produced annihilate with electrons). (i) Using the atomic masses ¹H = 1.007825 u and ⁴He = 4.002603 u, find the energy released per helium atom formed. (ii) The Sun radiates 3.8×10²⁶ W. Estimate the mass of hydrogen converted into helium every second. (iii) Why can this reaction take place only at temperatures of the order of 10⁷ K? (1 u = 931.5 MeV, 1 MeV = 1.6×10⁻¹³ J, mass of ¹H atom = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg)
items.ans:
(i) Δm = 4 × 1.007825 − 4.002603 = 0.028697 u; Q = 0.028697 × 931.5 ≈ 26.7 MeV. [1]
(ii) Energy per reaction = 26.7 × 1.6×10⁻¹³ ≈ 4.28×10⁻¹² J; reactions per second = 3.8×10²⁶/4.28×10⁻¹² ≈ 8.9×10³⁷. Hydrogen used = 4 × 8.9×10³⁷ × 1.67×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 5.9×10¹¹ kg per second (about 600 million tonnes). [1]
(iii) The nuclei are positively charged and repel each other strongly. Only at about 10⁷ K do enough of them have the kinetic energy needed to come within the short range (about 10⁻¹⁵ m) of the attractive nuclear force and fuse. [1]

items.q: A point charge q = 8.85 nC is placed at one corner of a cube. Find (i) the total electric flux through the cube, (ii) the flux through each of the three faces that do not touch the charge, (iii) the flux through each of the three faces that meet at the charge. Give reasons. (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
items.ans:
(i) Eight such cubes placed around the charge would enclose it completely, with total flux q/ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻⁹/8.85×10⁻¹² = 1000 N m² C⁻¹. By symmetry, one cube receives one-eighth: Φ = q/8ε₀ = 125 N m² C⁻¹. [1]
(ii) The field lines are radial from the corner, so they lie along the three faces meeting there; all the flux passes through the other three faces, which share it equally by symmetry: Φ = q/24ε₀ ≈ 41.7 N m² C⁻¹ each. [1]
(iii) Zero. On these faces the radial field is parallel to the surface (E ⟂ normal), so E·dS = 0. [1]

items.q: Three branches are connected in parallel between two junctions X and Y. Branch 1 has a 10 V battery of internal resistance 2 Ω; branch 2 has a 4 Ω resistor; branch 3 has a 5 V battery of internal resistance 1 Ω. Both batteries have their positive terminals towards X. Using Kirchhoff's rules, find (i) the current in each branch, (ii) the potential difference V_X − V_Y. (iii) Is either battery being charged?
items.ans:
Let V_X − V_Y = V. Junction rule at X: (10 − V)/2 + (5 − V)/1 = V/4 → 5 − V/2 + 5 − V = V/4 → 1.75V = 10 → V ≈ 5.71 V. [1]
(i) Branch 1: I₁ = (10 − 5.71)/2 ≈ 2.14 A (out of the + terminal towards X). Branch 3: I₃ = (5 − 5.71)/1 ≈ −0.71 A, i.e. 0.71 A flows from X into the + terminal of the 5 V battery. Branch 2: I₂ = 5.71/4 ≈ 1.43 A from X to Y. Check: 2.14 = 1.43 + 0.71. [1]
(ii) V_X − V_Y ≈ 5.71 V. (iii) Yes — current enters the 5 V battery at its positive terminal, so it is being charged by the 10 V battery. [1]

items.q: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 4.0 cm carries a current of 2.0 A and is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Find (i) the magnetic moment of the coil, (ii) the maximum torque on it, (iii) the work done in rotating it from its position of stable equilibrium to its position of unstable equilibrium.
items.ans:
(i) m = NIA = 50 × 2.0 × π(0.04)² ≈ 0.50 A m². [1]
(ii) τ_max = mB = 0.503 × 0.20 ≈ 0.10 N m (when the plane of the coil is parallel to B). [1]
(iii) U = −mB cos θ; stable equilibrium θ = 0 (U = −mB), unstable θ = 180° (U = +mB). W = 2mB = 2 × 0.503 × 0.20 ≈ 0.20 J. [1]

items.q: A coil draws a current of 2.0 A when connected to a 12 V DC supply, and a current of 1.2 A when connected to a 12 V (rms), 50 Hz AC supply. Find (i) the resistance and the impedance of the coil, (ii) its inductance, (iii) its power factor and the average power consumed on the AC supply.
items.ans:
(i) With DC there is no induced emf in steady state, so R = 12/2.0 = 6 Ω. On AC, Z = 12/1.2 = 10 Ω. [1]
(ii) X_L = √(Z² − R²) = √(100 − 36) = 8 Ω; L = X_L/(2πν) = 8/(2π × 50) ≈ 2.5×10⁻² H = 25 mH. [1]
(iii) cos φ = R/Z = 6/10 = 0.6; P = I²_rms R = 1.2² × 6 ≈ 8.6 W (= V I cos φ = 12 × 1.2 × 0.6). [1]

items.q: An equiconvex glass lens (μ = 1.5) has a focal length of 20 cm in air. (i) Find the radius of curvature of its surfaces. (ii) The lens is cut into two identical plano-convex halves by a plane perpendicular to its principal axis. Find the focal length of each half. (iii) Find the focal length and nature of the original lens when it is immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.65.
items.ans:
(i) 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/R − (−1/R)) = (0.5)(2/R) = 1/R → R = f = 20 cm. [1]
(ii) Each half has one curved surface: 1/f' = (0.5)(1/20) → f' = 40 cm. [1]
(iii) 1/f_l = (μ_g/μ_l − 1)(2/R) = (1.5/1.65 − 1)(2/20) = (−0.0909)(0.1) → f_l ≈ −110 cm. The lens now behaves as a diverging lens, because the liquid is optically denser than the glass. [1]

items.q: An X-ray photon and an electron each have a wavelength of 0.20 nm. (i) Compare their momenta. (ii) Find the energy of the photon and the kinetic energy of the electron, in eV. (iii) Use the result to explain why electron beams, rather than X-rays of the same wavelength, are often preferred for studying delicate surfaces. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3×10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
items.ans:
(i) p = h/λ for both, so the momenta are equal: p = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/0.20×10⁻⁹ ≈ 3.3×10⁻²⁴ kg m/s. [1]
(ii) Photon: E = hc/λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸/0.20×10⁻⁹ ≈ 9.9×10⁻¹⁶ J ≈ 6.2×10³ eV. Electron: K = p²/2m = (3.3×10⁻²⁴)²/(2 × 9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 6.0×10⁻¹⁸ J ≈ 38 eV. [1]
(iii) For the same wavelength (same ability to resolve detail), the electron carries only about 38 eV compared with about 6 keV for the photon, so it deposits far less energy in the sample and is much less likely to damage it. [1]

items.q: Using the atomic masses ¹H = 1.007825 u, n = 1.008665 u, ⁴He = 4.002603 u and ¹²C = 12.000000 u, find (i) the binding energy per nucleon of ¹²C, (ii) the minimum energy needed to break a ¹²C nucleus into three α-particles. (iii) Why is a ¹²C nucleus stable even though it can be thought of as made of three α-particles? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
items.ans:
(i) Δm = 6(1.007825) + 6(1.008665) − 12.000000 = 0.098940 u; BE = 0.098940 × 931.5 ≈ 92.2 MeV; BE per nucleon ≈ 7.68 MeV. [1]
(ii) Mass of three α-particles − mass of ¹²C = 3(4.002603) − 12.000000 = 0.007809 u → energy needed ≈ 0.007809 × 931.5 ≈ 7.27 MeV. [1]
(iii) The mass of ¹²C is less than that of three α-particles, so its total binding energy (92.2 MeV) exceeds that of three α-particles (3 × 28.3 ≈ 84.9 MeV). It cannot break up spontaneously into α-particles; about 7.3 MeV must be supplied. [1]

items.q:
[CBQ] Doping Silicon at a Chip Fab
A semiconductor fab coming up at Dholera, Gujarat, receives extremely pure silicon wafers. Engineers add tiny, controlled amounts of impurity atoms (about 1 impurity atom per 10⁷ silicon atoms) to create n-type and p-type regions.
(i) Name one impurity used to make n-type silicon and state its valency. [1m]
(ii) Why does a doped wafer conduct far better than pure silicon at room temperature, though the impurity is only 1 part in 10⁷? [1m]
(iii) In p-type silicon, which charge carriers are in majority? Is the crystal as a whole charged? [1m]
(iv) Where does the donor energy level lie in the energy band diagram of n-type silicon? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Phosphorus (or arsenic/antimony) — pentavalent (valency 5).
(ii) Each donor atom easily gives one free electron at room temperature; 1 in 10⁷ of ~5×10²⁸ Si atoms/m³ gives ~5×10²¹ electrons/m³, far more than the intrinsic carrier density (~10¹⁶ m⁻³).
(iii) Holes are majority carriers. The crystal is electrically neutral overall (charge of holes is balanced by the fixed negative acceptor ions).
(iv) Just below the bottom of the conduction band (about 0.01–0.05 eV below it), inside the band gap.

items.q:
[CBQ] Photoelectric Effect Investigation
A lab uses UV light on sodium surface (work function φ₀ = 2 eV). Experiment varies frequency and intensity.
(i) Define work function. [1m]
(ii) Explain why increasing intensity increases photocurrent but not KE. [1m]
(iii) Light of frequency 1.2×10¹⁵ Hz hits the surface. Find maximum KE. [1m]
(iv) State two observations of the photoelectric effect that CANNOT be explained by the wave theory of light. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Work function: minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface.
(ii) More intensity = more photons per second → more electrons emitted → more current. But each photon's energy hν depends only on frequency, so KE_max is unchanged.
(iii) E = hν = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 1.2×10¹⁵ J ≈ 4.96 eV. KE_max = E − φ₀ ≈ 4.96 − 2 ≈ 2.96 eV (≈ 3 eV).
(iv) (a) KE_max depends on frequency, not on intensity; (b) emission is instantaneous, with no time lag even for very dim light (also: existence of a threshold frequency).

items.q:
[CBQ] Optical Fibres for Village Internet
Under the BharatNet project, optical fibre cables carry internet to gram panchayats. Each fibre has a glass core of refractive index 1.50 surrounded by a cladding of refractive index 1.45. Light signals travel kilometres through the core with very little loss.
(i) Name the phenomenon that keeps light inside the core. [1m]
(ii) Why must the cladding have a lower refractive index than the core? [1m]
(iii) Find the critical angle at the core–cladding interface. [1m]
(iv) A ray inside the core strikes the core–cladding interface at an angle of incidence of 70°. Will it be guided along the fibre? Give reason. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Total internal reflection.
(ii) TIR is possible only when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium, so the cladding must be optically rarer (lower μ) than the core.
(iii) sin C = μ_cladding/μ_core = 1.45/1.50 ≈ 0.967 → C ≈ 75.2°.
(iv) No. 70° is less than the critical angle 75.2°, so the ray is partly refracted into the cladding and the signal leaks out instead of being totally reflected.

items.q:
[CBQ] Inside a Phone Charger
A student in a hostel opens an old mobile charger. It has a small step-down transformer, two diodes connected as a centre-tap full-wave rectifier, and a capacitor across the output. The mains supply is 230 V, 50 Hz.
(i) What property of a p-n junction diode makes it useful for rectification? [1m]
(ii) What is the frequency of the ripple in the rectified output? [1m]
(iii) How many diodes conduct during each half-cycle of the input? [1m]
(iv) What is the role of the capacitor connected across the output? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) It conducts (low resistance) only in forward bias and offers very high resistance in reverse bias — current flows in one direction only.
(ii) Full-wave rectifier: ripple frequency = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.
(iii) One diode conducts in each half-cycle (the two diodes conduct alternately), so current through the load is always in the same direction.
(iv) It acts as a filter: it charges near the peak and discharges slowly through the load, smoothing the pulsating DC into nearly steady DC.

items.q:
[CBQ] Spectacles for the Back Bench
Riya, a Class XII student in Pune, cannot read the board clearly from the last bench. An optometrist prescribes spectacles of power −0.5 D. Her grandfather uses reading glasses of power +2.5 D.
(i) What is the nature and focal length of Riya's lens? [1m]
(ii) Where does her lens form the image of a very distant object? [1m]
(iii) Riya looks through her lens at a notice board 6 m away. Find the position of the image. [1m]
(iv) If Riya's lens and her grandfather's lens are held in contact, what is the power of the combination? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Diverging (concave) lens; f = 1/P = 1/(−0.5) m = −2 m (−200 cm).
(ii) At its focus — a virtual, erect, diminished image 2 m in front of the lens (same side as the object).
(iii) 1/v − 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/(−2) + 1/(−6) = −2/3 → v = −1.5 m: virtual image 1.5 m in front of the lens.
(iv) P = P₁ + P₂ = −0.5 + 2.5 = +2.0 D (converging, f = 50 cm).

items.q:
[CBQ] Diode Characteristics in the School Lab
Students in a Lucknow school lab record the forward characteristic of a silicon diode. The current is almost zero up to about 0.6 V and then rises sharply: at 0.70 V it is 10 mA and at 0.75 V it is 30 mA.
(i) What is the threshold (knee) voltage, and why is the current nearly zero below it? [1m]
(ii) Find the dynamic resistance of the diode between 0.70 V and 0.75 V. [1m]
(iii) How does the width of the depletion layer change when the forward voltage is increased? [1m]
(iv) Why is the diode called a non-ohmic device? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) About 0.7 V for silicon. Below it the applied voltage cannot overcome the barrier potential, so very few majority carriers cross the junction.
(ii) r_d = ΔV/ΔI = (0.75 − 0.70)/(30 − 10)×10⁻³ = 0.05/0.020 = 2.5 Ω.
(iii) It decreases — the forward voltage opposes the barrier potential, so the depletion layer becomes narrower.
(iv) Its V–I graph is not a straight line (current does not vary linearly with voltage) and it conducts differently in forward and reverse bias, so Ohm's law is not obeyed.

items.q:
[CBQ] Prism Periscope in an Army Bunker
Soldiers at a border post in Ladakh observe the area from inside a bunker using a periscope. Instead of plane mirrors, it uses two right-angled isosceles glass prisms (refractive index 1.5). Light enters one face normally and meets the hypotenuse face at an angle of incidence of 45°.
(i) Name the phenomenon that turns the light through 90° in each prism. [1m]
(ii) Find the critical angle for the glass–air surface. [1m]
(iii) Would the periscope still work if the prisms were made of a material of refractive index 1.3? Give reason. [1m]
(iv) Give one advantage of using such prisms in place of plane mirrors. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Total internal reflection at the hypotenuse face.
(ii) sin C = 1/μ = 1/1.5 = 0.667 → C ≈ 41.8°.
(iii) No. For μ = 1.3, C = sin⁻¹(1/1.3) ≈ 50.3°; the angle of incidence 45° is less than C, so the light would be partly refracted out instead of being totally reflected.
(iv) TIR reflects almost 100% of the light (brighter image), and there is no silvering to tarnish or peel off; no multiple images as in a thick glass mirror.

items.q:
[CBQ] Temperature Sensor in a Baby Incubator
A primary health centre in Odisha uses baby incubators whose temperature is controlled by a sensor made of a semiconductor. As the semiconductor warms up, its resistance falls noticeably, and the control circuit switches the heater off. The band gap of the material is about 1.1 eV.
(i) Why does the resistance of a semiconductor fall when its temperature rises? [1m]
(ii) In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, how does the number of free electrons compare with the number of holes? [1m]
(iii) Can a photon of wavelength 600 nm create an electron–hole pair in this material? Show by calculation. [1m]
(iv) Find the longest wavelength of light that can create an electron–hole pair in this material. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) More electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the band gap into the conduction band, creating more electron–hole pairs; the increase in carriers far outweighs the small fall in mobility, so resistance falls.
(ii) They are equal (n_e = n_h = n_i), since each electron that crosses the gap leaves one hole behind.
(iii) E = hc/λ ≈ 1240/600 ≈ 2.07 eV, which is more than 1.1 eV, so yes, it can.
(iv) λ_max = hc/E_g ≈ 1240/1.1 ≈ 1130 nm (≈ 1.13 μm, in the infrared).

items.q:
[CBQ] Fuel for a Nuclear Power Station
The Kudankulam power station in Tamil Nadu produces electricity from the fission of uranium-235. A typical fission is ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n, and each fission releases about 200 MeV. Consider a reactor that produces 3000 MW of heat. (1 MeV = 1.6×10⁻¹³ J, Avogadro number = 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹)
(i) Why is energy released when a heavy nucleus splits into two medium-mass nuclei? [1m]
(ii) How many fissions take place every second in this reactor? [1m]
(iii) Estimate the mass of U-235 used up in one day. [1m]
(iv) How much mass is converted into energy in one day? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) The fission fragments have a higher binding energy per nucleon (≈ 8.5 MeV) than U-235 (≈ 7.6 MeV); the increase in total binding energy is released (mass defect → energy).
(ii) Energy per fission = 200 × 1.6×10⁻¹³ = 3.2×10⁻¹¹ J. Fissions per second = 3×10⁹/3.2×10⁻¹¹ ≈ 9.4×10¹⁹ s⁻¹.
(iii) Per day: 9.375×10¹⁹ × 86400 ≈ 8.1×10²⁴ nuclei; mass = (8.1×10²⁴/6.022×10²³) × 235 g ≈ 3.2×10³ g ≈ 3.2 kg.
(iv) Energy per day = 3×10⁹ × 86400 ≈ 2.6×10¹⁴ J; Δm = E/c² = 2.6×10¹⁴/(9×10¹⁶) ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ kg ≈ 2.9 g.

items.q:
[CBQ] The Jeweller's Magnifier
A goldsmith in Jaipur checks the hallmark on a gold ring using a small magnifying glass (a convex lens of focal length 5 cm) held close to his eye. His near point is 25 cm.
(i) Find the magnifying power when the final image is formed at his near point. [1m]
(ii) Find the magnifying power when the image is at infinity (relaxed eye). [1m]
(iii) How far from the lens should the ring be held so that the image forms at 25 cm? [1m]
(iv) Why would a lens of focal length 2.5 cm suit him better for very fine engraving? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) m = 1 + D/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6.
(ii) m = D/f = 25/5 = 5.
(iii) v = −25 cm, f = +5 cm: 1/u = 1/v − 1/f = −1/25 − 1/5 = −6/25 → u ≈ −4.17 cm, i.e. about 4.2 cm in front of the lens (just inside the focus).
(iv) Magnifying power ∝ 1/f: with f = 2.5 cm, m = 1 + 25/2.5 = 11 (or 10 at infinity), so finer details look larger.

items.q:
[CBQ] Underwater Lights at a Swimming Pool
A public swimming pool in Bengaluru has small lamps fixed on its floor, 2 m below the water surface (μ of water = 4/3). At night, a swimmer standing outside notices that each lamp lights up a bright circular patch on the surface, while the surface outside this patch looks dark from above.
(i) Find the critical angle for the water–air surface. [1m]
(ii) Find the radius of the bright circle on the surface above one lamp. [1m]
(iii) Why does no light from the lamp come out of the surface outside this circle? [1m]
(iv) At what depth does the lamp appear to a person looking vertically down on it? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) sin C = 1/μ = 3/4 = 0.75 → C ≈ 48.6°.
(ii) Light escapes only for angles of incidence up to C: r = h tan C = 2 × tan 48.6° ≈ 2 × 1.134 ≈ 2.27 m.
(iii) Rays meeting the surface outside the circle have angle of incidence greater than C, so they undergo total internal reflection back into the water.
(iv) Apparent depth = real depth/μ = 2 × 3/4 = 1.5 m.

items.q:
[CBQ] Hydrogen Discharge Tube in the Physics Lab
In a school lab in Bhopal, a hydrogen discharge tube is viewed through a spectroscope. In the tube, collisions excite hydrogen atoms from the ground state up to the n = 4 level, and the atoms then return to lower levels. (Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, hc = 1240 eV nm)
(i) How many different spectral lines can be emitted? [1m]
(ii) Find the longest wavelength in the Lyman series and name its region. [1m]
(iii) Which of the emitted lines can the students see with their eyes? Give their wavelengths. [1m]
(iv) How much energy is needed to ionise an atom that is in the n = 2 state? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Number of lines = n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.
(ii) Longest Lyman wavelength: n = 2 → 1, ΔE = 13.6(1 − 1/4) = 10.2 eV; λ = 1240/10.2 ≈ 121.6 nm — ultraviolet.
(iii) The Balmer lines (ending on n = 2) from n = 3 and n = 4: ΔE = 1.89 eV → λ ≈ 656 nm (red) and ΔE = 2.55 eV → λ ≈ 486 nm (blue-green).
(iv) E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV, so 3.4 eV is needed.

items.q:
[CBQ] Mirage on a Summer Highway
Driving on the Agra–Lucknow Expressway on a hot May afternoon, a family sees what looks like a pool of water on the road far ahead, with an inverted image of a truck in it. As they come closer, the 'water' disappears. The air just above the hot road is much hotter than the air higher up.
(i) Why is the refractive index of the air layer just above the road lower than that of the air higher up? [1m]
(ii) Name the phenomenon that finally sends light from the sky (or the truck) back up towards the observer's eyes. [1m]
(iii) Take the refractive index of the air higher up as 1.000280 and that of the layer at the road surface as 1.000250. Find the critical angle for light going from the upper layer into the lower layer. [1m]
(iv) Use your answer to (iii) to explain why the mirage is seen only far ahead on the road, and not close to the car. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Hot air is less dense (it expands), and the refractive index of air decreases as its density decreases.
(ii) Total internal reflection (after gradual bending away from the normal as light passes into hotter, optically rarer layers).
(iii) sin C = 1.000250/1.000280 ≈ 0.99997 → C ≈ 89.6°.
(iv) TIR needs an angle of incidence greater than about 89.6°, i.e. light must travel almost parallel (grazing) to the road. Such rays reach the eye only from points far ahead; rays from the road close to the car strike the layers too steeply and pass through.

items.q:
[CBQ] Checking Diodes at a Repair Shop
A technician at an electronics repair shop in Chennai tests silicon diodes taken out of old chargers. With a multimeter on the resistance setting, a good diode shows a low reading when connected one way and a very high reading when the leads are reversed. The cathode end of each diode is marked with a silver band.
(i) Why does a good diode give very different readings in the two directions? [1m]
(ii) To forward bias the diode with a battery, which terminal should the banded end be connected to? [1m]
(iii) One diode shows a very low reading in both directions. What fault does this indicate? [1m]
(iv) A good diode (0.7 V drop when conducting) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 9 V battery. Find the current. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) In forward bias the barrier is lowered and majority carriers cross easily (low resistance); in reverse bias the barrier is raised and only a tiny minority-carrier current flows (very high resistance) — the diode conducts in one direction only.
(ii) The banded (cathode, n-side) end goes to the negative terminal; the p-side (anode) to the positive terminal.
(iii) The junction is damaged (short-circuited / broken down): it no longer blocks current in reverse, so the diode is faulty.
(iv) I = (9 − 0.7)/1000 = 8.3×10⁻³ A = 8.3 mA.

items.q:
[CBQ] The Door Viewer
The front door of a flat in Mumbai has a small door viewer ('magic eye') so that the family can see who is outside before opening the door. In a simple model, the viewer is a single diverging lens of focal length 2 cm. A visitor 1.6 m tall stands 1.0 m from the lens.
(i) Why is a diverging lens used, rather than a converging lens? [1m]
(ii) Find the position of the image of the visitor. [1m]
(iii) Find the height of the image and state its nature. [1m]
(iv) If the lens were replaced by a diverging lens of focal length 1 cm, would the image of the visitor be larger or smaller? Justify. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) A diverging lens always forms an erect, diminished, virtual image of objects at any distance and gives a wide field of view, so the whole visitor can be seen through a tiny hole.
(ii) f = −2 cm, u = −100 cm: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = −1/2 − 1/100 = −0.51 → v ≈ −1.96 cm, i.e. about 2 cm from the lens on the visitor's side.
(iii) m = v/u = (−1.96)/(−100) ≈ 0.0196 → image height ≈ 0.0196 × 160 cm ≈ 3.1 cm; virtual, erect and diminished.
(iv) Smaller: 1/v = −1 − 1/100 → v ≈ −0.99 cm, m ≈ 0.0099, image ≈ 1.6 cm tall. A shorter focal length gives a smaller image (but an even wider view).

items.q:
[CBQ] Why Is a Silicon Wafer Not Transparent?
At a solar-panel factory in Noida, visitors notice that polished silicon wafers look grey and opaque, while the glass sheets covering the panels are transparent. A guide explains that this depends on the band gap: silicon has E_g ≈ 1.1 eV, diamond about 5.5 eV, and glass is also a wide-gap insulator. Photons of visible light have energies from about 1.8 eV (red) to 3.1 eV (violet). (hc = 1240 eV nm)
(i) Why does silicon absorb all visible light? [1m]
(ii) Find the longest wavelength that can create an electron–hole pair in silicon. In which region of the spectrum is it? [1m]
(iii) Explain why diamond is transparent to visible light. [1m]
(iv) Why does the conductivity of silicon increase with temperature, while that of copper decreases? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Every visible photon has energy (1.8–3.1 eV) greater than the band gap of 1.1 eV, so it can lift a valence electron into the conduction band and is absorbed.
(ii) λ_max = hc/E_g = 1240/1.1 ≈ 1.13×10³ nm (about 1130 nm) — in the near-infrared.
(iii) Diamond's gap of 5.5 eV needs λ ≤ 1240/5.5 ≈ 225 nm (ultraviolet). Visible photons do not have enough energy to cross the gap, so they are not absorbed and pass through.
(iv) In silicon, more electrons are thermally excited across the gap as temperature rises, so the number of charge carriers increases sharply. In copper the number of free electrons is fixed; heating only increases collisions (shorter relaxation time), so resistivity rises.

items.q:
[CBQ] The Slide Projector in the School Hall
For a science exhibition in a school in Guwahati, students use an old slide projector. Its convex projection lens forms a sharp image of a 3.5 cm tall slide on a screen 5 m from the lens. The picture on the screen is 1.4 m tall.
(i) Find the magnification and state the nature of the image. [1m]
(ii) How far from the lens is the slide? [1m]
(iii) Find the focal length of the projection lens. [1m]
(iv) Why must the slide be placed upside down in the projector? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) |m| = 140 cm/3.5 cm = 40. The image is formed on a screen, so it is real and inverted: m = −40.
(ii) m = v/u → u = v/m = 500/(−40) = −12.5 cm: the slide is 12.5 cm from the lens.
(iii) 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/500 + 1/12.5 = 0.002 + 0.08 = 0.082 → f ≈ 12.2 cm.
(iv) A convex lens forms a real image that is inverted with respect to the object, so the slide is put in upside down to obtain an erect picture on the screen.

items.q:
[CBQ] A Diode in a Solar Lantern
A solar lantern used in a village in Rajasthan charges a 6.0 V battery from a small solar panel. A silicon diode (forward voltage drop 0.7 V) is connected in series between the panel and the battery, with its p-side towards the panel's positive terminal. In bright sunlight the panel gives 7.2 V. The total resistance of the wires and the battery in the charging circuit is 1.0 Ω.
(i) Find the charging current in bright sunlight. [1m]
(ii) How much power is wasted in the diode while charging? [1m]
