(iii) At night the panel gives no voltage. What is the state of the diode then, and why is the diode needed at all? [1m]
(iv) What would happen if the diode were connected the other way round? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) The diode is forward biased: I = (7.2 − 0.7 − 6.0)/1.0 = 0.5 A.
(ii) P = V_D × I = 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.35 W.
(iii) The battery now makes the n-side more positive than the p-side, so the diode is reverse biased and only a negligible reverse current flows. It prevents the battery from discharging back through the panel at night (it lets current flow in one direction only).
(iv) The diode would be reverse biased in sunlight, so the battery would not charge at all (only a tiny reverse saturation current would flow).

items.q:
[CBQ] The Dentist's Mirror
A dentist in Kolkata examines a patient's back tooth with a small concave mirror of focal length 3.0 cm fixed on a thin handle. She holds the mirror 2.0 cm from the tooth so that she sees an enlarged view of it.
(i) Find the position of the image of the tooth formed by the mirror. [1m]
(ii) Find the magnification and state whether the image is real or virtual, erect or inverted. [1m]
(iii) Why is a concave mirror used for this purpose and not a convex mirror? [1m]
(iv) If the dentist moves the mirror so that it is 4.0 cm from the tooth, what kind of image is formed now, and why is this not useful to her? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) u = −2.0 cm, f = −3.0 cm: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/3 + 1/2 = 1/6 → v = +6.0 cm, i.e. 6 cm behind the mirror.
(ii) m = −v/u = −(6)/(−2) = +3: the image is virtual, erect and three times enlarged.
(iii) A concave mirror gives an erect, magnified image when the object is within its focal length; a convex mirror always gives a diminished image, which would show less detail.
(iv) 1/v = −1/3 + 1/4 = −1/12 → v = −12 cm, m = −3: the image is real and inverted, formed 12 cm in front of the mirror. She would no longer see an erect, magnified view of the tooth in the mirror, so the mirror must be held closer to the tooth than its focal length (3 cm).

items.q:
[CBQ] Choosing Diodes for a Desert Weather Station
An automatic weather station is being installed in the Thar desert, where the electronics box can reach 70 °C in summer. An engineer compares a germanium diode (band gap about 0.7 eV, knee voltage about 0.3 V) with a silicon diode (band gap about 1.1 eV, knee voltage about 0.7 V). In one part of the circuit a diode is forward biased in series with a 100 Ω resistor across a 1.5 V cell. (Treat each diode as having a constant voltage drop equal to its knee voltage when conducting.)
(i) Why is the knee voltage of germanium lower than that of silicon? [1m]
(ii) Find the current in the circuit with the germanium diode. [1m]
(iii) Find the current with the silicon diode. [1m]
(iv) Why does the engineer choose silicon diodes for the hot desert station? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) Germanium has a smaller band gap, so the barrier potential at its p-n junction is smaller; a smaller forward voltage is enough to overcome it.
(ii) I = (1.5 − 0.3)/100 = 0.012 A = 12 mA.
(iii) I = (1.5 − 0.7)/100 = 0.008 A = 8 mA.
(iv) Because of its larger band gap, far fewer electron–hole pairs are generated thermally in silicon at high temperature, so its reverse (leakage) current stays very small and it keeps working as a reliable one-way device; germanium's leakage current becomes too large when hot.

items.q:
[CBQ] The Camera in a Smartphone
A student in Shillong photographs her friend, who is 1.70 m tall and stands 2.0 m away, using her phone camera. In a simple model, the camera has a single convex lens of focal length 4.0 mm that forms a real image on the image sensor behind it.
(i) Find the distance between the lens and the sensor for a sharp picture of the friend. [1m]
(ii) Find the magnification and the height of the image on the sensor. [1m]
(iii) Is the image on the sensor erect or inverted? How does the phone still show an upright picture? [1m]
(iv) She now photographs a flower 10 cm from the lens. By how much, and in which direction, must the lens move to keep the image sharp? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) u = −2000 mm, f = 4.0 mm: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/4 − 1/2000 → v ≈ 4.008 mm (just beyond the focal point).
(ii) m = v/u = 4.008/(−2000) ≈ −0.002; image height = 0.002 × 1700 mm ≈ 3.4 mm.
(iii) The real image formed by a single convex lens is inverted; the phone's software simply flips the picture electronically before displaying it.
(iv) For u = −100 mm: 1/v = 1/4 − 1/100 → v ≈ 4.167 mm. The lens must move about 4.167 − 4.008 ≈ 0.16 mm farther away from the sensor (closer objects form images farther from the lens).

items.q:
[CBQ] Doping Germanium for a Sensor Lab
At a materials laboratory in Bengaluru, a pure germanium crystal (about 4.4×10²⁸ atoms per m³, intrinsic carrier concentration 2.4×10¹⁹ m⁻³ at 300 K) is doped with indium at the level of one indium atom per million germanium atoms.
(i) Is the doped crystal n-type or p-type? Give a reason. [1m]
(ii) Estimate the concentration of the majority carriers. [1m]
(iii) Using n_e n_h = n_i², find the concentration of the minority carriers. [1m]
(iv) Why does the minority-carrier concentration fall below its intrinsic value after doping? [1m]
items.ans:
(i) p-type: indium is trivalent, so each indium atom forms only three covalent bonds and creates a hole (it is an acceptor).
(ii) N_A = 4.4×10²⁸ × 10⁻⁶ = 4.4×10²² m⁻³; since N_A ≫ n_i, the hole concentration n_h ≈ 4.4×10²² m⁻³.
(iii) n_e = n_i²/n_h = (2.4×10¹⁹)²/4.4×10²² ≈ 1.3×10¹⁶ m⁻³.
(iv) With so many holes present, thermally generated electrons recombine with holes much more often, so the equilibrium electron concentration is pushed far below n_i (the product n_e n_h stays fixed at n_i²).

items.q:
(A) A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area A separated by d, with dielectric K between them.
(i) An isolated conductor always has small capacitance — why? [2m]
(ii) Three capacitors 6μF, 9μF, 18μF: find minimum and maximum capacitance. [2m]
(iii) Two other factors (besides area) on which capacitance depends. [1m]
items.ans:
(i) C = 4πε₀R for isolated sphere → depends only on radius. Very large capacitance needs impractically large sphere.
(ii) Min (series): 1/C = 1/6+1/9+1/18 = 6/18 → C_min = 3 μF.
    Max (parallel): C_max = 6+9+18 = 33 μF.
(iii) Distance between plates (C ∝ 1/d), dielectric constant of the medium between the plates (C ∝ K).
items.orq:
(B) Two long parallel wires carry currents I₁ and I₂ separated by distance d.
(i) Derive expression for force per unit length between them. [3m]
(ii) State condition for attraction/repulsion. [1m]
(iii) Define 1 Ampere using this force law. [1m]
items.orans:
(i) B₁ = μ₀I₁/2πd. Force on length L of wire 2: F = I₂LB₁ = μ₀I₁I₂L/2πd. Per unit length: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd.
(ii) Same direction currents → attract; opposite directions → repel.
(iii) 1 A is that current which, when flowing in each of two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces force of 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre length.

items.q:
(A) Explain Young's Double Slit Experiment:
(i) Derive expression for fringe width β. [3m]
(ii) What happens to fringe width if: (a) slit separation halved (b) screen distance doubled. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Path difference = dy/D (d=slit sep, y=position, D=screen dist). For bright: dy/D = nλ → y_n = nλD/d. Fringe width β = λD/d.
(ii) (a) d→d/2 → β doubles. (b) D→2D → β doubles.
items.orq:
(B) (i) Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion with one example each. [2m]
(ii) In fission of U-235, about 0.1% mass converts to energy. Energy from 1 kg? [3m]
items.orans:
(i) Fission: heavy nucleus splits → lighter nuclei + energy. E.g., U-235 + n → Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n.
Fusion: light nuclei combine → heavier nucleus + energy. E.g., ²H+³H → ⁴He + n.
(ii) E = mc² = 0.001×1×(3×10⁸)² = 9×10¹³ J.

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive the lens maker's formula 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) for a thin double-convex lens. [3m]
(ii) A double-convex lens of glass (μ = 1.5) has radii of curvature 20 cm and 30 cm. Find its focal length and power in air. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Refraction at first surface (object O in air, image I₁): μ/v₁ − 1/u = (μ − 1)/R₁.
I₁ acts as object for second surface (glass to air): 1/v − μ/v₁ = (1 − μ)/R₂.
Adding: 1/v − 1/u = (μ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). For u = ∞, v = f → 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). [3]
(ii) R₁ = +20 cm, R₂ = −30 cm: 1/f = 0.5(1/20 + 1/30) = 0.5 × 1/12 = 1/24 → f = 24 cm. [1]
P = 100/f(cm) = 100/24 ≈ +4.17 D. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State and prove Ampere's circuital law. [3m]
(ii) A solenoid 1m long, 1000 turns carries 2A. Find B inside. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed. For a closed loop, circulation of B = μ₀ × current enclosed.
Proof for infinite wire: By symmetry B is tangential, constant on circular path of radius r. B×2πr = μ₀I → B = μ₀I/2πr.
(ii) B = μ₀nI = μ₀(N/L)I = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 2 = 8π×10⁻⁴ T ≈ 2.51×10⁻³ T.

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor (plate area A, separation d) when a dielectric slab of dielectric constant K and thickness t (t less than d) is placed between the plates. [3m]
(ii) A capacitor has plate area 0.02 m² and separation 4 mm. A slab of thickness 2 mm and K = 4 is inserted. Find its capacitance. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Field in air gaps E₀ = σ/ε₀; inside slab E = E₀/K. Potential difference V = E₀(d − t) + (E₀/K)t = (σ/ε₀)(d − t + t/K). [2]
C = Q/V = σA/V = ε₀A/(d − t + t/K). [1]
(ii) C = (8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.02)/(0.004 − 0.002 + 0.002/4) = 1.77×10⁻¹³/0.0025 ≈ 7.08×10⁻¹¹ F ≈ 70.8 pF. [2]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the axial line of an electric dipole and show that for r much greater than a, E = 2kp/r³. [3m]
(ii) Charges ±5 nC are 2 mm apart. Find the electric field at 10 cm from the centre of the dipole (a) on its axis, (b) on its equatorial line. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Charges −q at A and +q at B, separation 2a; point P on axis at distance r from centre. E₊ = kq/(r − a)², E₋ = kq/(r + a)² (opposite). [1]
E = kq[1/(r − a)² − 1/(r + a)²] = kq·4ar/(r² − a²)² = 2kpr/(r² − a²)², along p (p = 2aq). [1]
For r ≫ a: E = 2kp/r³. [1]
(ii) p = 5×10⁻⁹ × 2×10⁻³ = 10⁻¹¹ C m. (a) E_axial = 2kp/r³ = 2 × 9×10⁹ × 10⁻¹¹/(0.1)³ = 180 N/C. [1]
(b) E_equatorial = kp/r³ = 90 N/C, directed opposite to p. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) State the principle of a transformer and, for an ideal transformer, derive V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. [3m]
(ii) A transformer steps 220 V mains down to 11 V for a set of LED lamps in a shop. The primary has 2200 turns. Find the number of secondary turns. If the secondary current is 4 A and the efficiency is 90%, find the primary current. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Principle: mutual induction — an alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux in the core that induces an emf in the secondary. [1]
Same flux φ links each turn: ε_p = −N_p dφ/dt, ε_s = −N_s dφ/dt. [1]
For ideal transformer (no losses, negligible resistance) V_p ≈ ε_p, V_s ≈ ε_s → V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. [1]
(ii) N_s = 2200 × 11/220 = 110 turns. [1]
P_out = 11 × 4 = 44 W; P_in = 44/0.9 ≈ 48.9 W → I_p = 48.9/220 ≈ 0.22 A. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Using the Biot–Savart law, derive an expression for the magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop of radius R at a distance x from its centre. [3m]
(ii) A coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm carries 2 A. Find the magnetic field at its centre and at a point on its axis 10 cm from the centre. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Element dl at the loop; distance to P is r = √(R² + x²), dl ⊥ r. dB = μ₀I dl/(4πr²). [1]
Components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs; axial components add: dB_x = dB·R/r. [1]
B = (μ₀IR/(4πr³))·2πR = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)], along the axis. [1]
(ii) Centre: B = μ₀NI/(2R) = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 50 × 2)/(0.2) ≈ 6.28×10⁻⁴ T. [1]
At x = R: B = B_centre/(2)^(3/2) ≈ 6.28×10⁻⁴/2.83 ≈ 2.22×10⁻⁴ T. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Draw a labelled ray diagram of an astronomical refracting telescope in normal adjustment and derive an expression for its magnifying power. [3m]
(ii) A telescope has an objective of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. Find its magnifying power and length in normal adjustment. Why is the objective made of large aperture? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Ray diagram: parallel rays from a distant object pass through the objective (large f₀) and form a real, inverted image at its focus, which is also the focus of the eyepiece; rays emerge parallel, final image at infinity. [1]
Object subtends α at objective; final image subtends β at eye. tan α ≈ α = h/f₀, tan β ≈ β = h/f_e (h = size of intermediate image). [1]
m = β/α = f₀/f_e. [1]
(ii) m = 150/5 = 30; length L = f₀ + f_e = 155 cm. [1]
Large aperture gathers more light (brighter image) and gives better resolution of distant objects. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Explain the formation of the diffraction pattern due to a single slit illuminated by monochromatic light and show that the angular width of the central maximum is 2λ/a. [3m]
(ii) Light of wavelength 500 nm falls on a slit of width 0.2 mm; the screen is 2 m away. Find the linear width of the central maximum. What happens to this width if the slit width is doubled? [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Each point of the slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens). At θ = 0 all wavelets are in phase → bright central maximum. [1]
Divide the slit into two halves: at a sin θ = λ each point of the upper half has a partner in the lower half with path difference λ/2 → cancellation → first minimum. Minima at a sin θ = nλ; secondary maxima (fainter) roughly at a sin θ = (n + ½)λ. [1]
Central maximum lies between θ = ±λ/a → angular width = 2λ/a. [1]
(ii) Linear width = 2λD/a = (2 × 500×10⁻⁹ × 2)/(0.2×10⁻³) = 0.01 m = 10 mm. [1]
If a is doubled, the width is halved (5 mm) — the pattern becomes narrower. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Obtain the relation I = neAv_d between current and drift velocity of free electrons in a conductor. Hence show that resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ). [3m]
(ii) A copper wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² carries a current of 1.5 A. The free-electron density of copper is 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³. Find the drift velocity. Why does a bulb glow almost instantly even though this speed is so small? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) In time Δt, electrons within length v_dΔt cross a section: charge = neA v_dΔt. I = q/Δt = neAv_d. [1]
v_d = eEτ/m and E = V/l → I = neA(eVτ/(ml)) → V/I = R = ml/(ne²τA). [1]
Comparing with R = ρl/A: ρ = m/(ne²τ). [1]
(ii) v_d = I/(neA) = 1.5/(8.5×10²⁸ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁴ m/s (≈ 0.11 mm/s). [1]
The electric field is set up along the whole circuit almost at the speed of light, so free electrons everywhere start drifting at once. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Using Gauss's law, find the electric field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R at (a) a point outside, (b) a point inside the shell. [3m]
(ii) A thin spherical shell of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 4 nC. Find the electric field at 5 cm and at 20 cm from its centre, and the surface charge density. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) (a) Outside (r greater than R): concentric Gaussian sphere of radius r; by symmetry E is radial and uniform on it. E·4πr² = q/ε₀ → E = q/(4πε₀r²), as if the whole charge were at the centre. [2]
(b) Inside (r less than R): Gaussian sphere encloses no charge → E·4πr² = 0 → E = 0. [1]
(ii) At 5 cm (inside): E = 0. At 20 cm: E = kq/r² = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁹/(0.2)² = 900 N/C, radially outward. [1]
σ = q/(4πR²) = 4×10⁻⁹/(4π × 0.01) ≈ 3.18×10⁻⁸ C/m². [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Using a phasor diagram, derive expressions for the impedance of a series LCR circuit and the phase angle between voltage and current. [3m]
(ii) A series circuit has R = 60 Ω, X_L = 120 Ω and X_C = 40 Ω, connected to a 220 V (rms) AC supply. Find the impedance, rms current and average power consumed. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Current I is common. V_R in phase with I, V_L leads I by 90°, V_C lags I by 90°. [1]
Resultant V = √[V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²] = I√[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] → Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]. [1]
tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R; voltage leads current if X_L is greater than X_C. [1]
(ii) Z = √[60² + (120 − 40)²] = √(3600 + 6400) = 100 Ω; I_rms = 220/100 = 2.2 A. [1]
cos φ = R/Z = 0.6; P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = 220 × 2.2 × 0.6 ≈ 290 W (= I²R = 4.84 × 60). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Describe the principle of an AC generator and show that the emf induced in its coil is e = NBAω sin ωt. [3m]
(ii) A coil of 100 turns and area 0.05 m² rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. Find the peak and rms values of the induced emf. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Principle: electromagnetic induction — when a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the flux linked with it changes and an emf is induced. [1]
At time t the normal to the coil makes angle θ = ωt with B: flux linkage = NBA cos ωt. [1]
e = −d(NBA cos ωt)/dt = NBAω sin ωt; peak e₀ = NBAω. [1]
(ii) ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad/s; e₀ = 100 × 0.1 × 0.05 × 314 ≈ 157 V. [1]
e_rms = e₀/√2 ≈ 111 V. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Draw a ray diagram for a concave mirror forming a real image of an object placed beyond C, and derive the mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. [3m]
(ii) The rear-view mirror of a bus is a convex mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm. An object 2 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of it. Find the position, nature and size of the image. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Ray parallel to axis reflects through F; ray through C retraces; they meet at the real, inverted image A'B'. Triangles A'B'F and MPF (paraxial, P ≈ M) are similar: A'B'/AB = B'F/FP. Triangles A'B'P and ABP: A'B'/AB = B'P/BP. [1]
So B'F/FP = B'P/BP → (v − f)/f = v/u using sign convention (u, v, f negative). [1]
Rearranging: uv − uf = vf → dividing by uvf: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. [1]
(ii) f = +20 cm, u = −30 cm: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/(−30) = 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 → v = +12 cm (behind the mirror). [1]
m = −v/u = −12/(−30) = +0.4 → image is virtual, erect, diminished, height 0.8 cm. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Draw a ray diagram of a compound microscope forming the final image at the least distance of distinct vision D and derive an expression for its magnifying power. [3m]
(ii) A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.25 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. An object is placed 1.5 cm from the objective and the final image is formed at 25 cm. Find the magnifying power and the separation of the lenses. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Objective (short f₀) forms a real, inverted, magnified image A'B' just inside the focus of the eyepiece; the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier forming the final virtual image at D. [1]
m_o = v_o/u_o (≈ L/f₀ for the image near the eyepiece focus); m_e = 1 + D/f_e. [1]
M = m_o × m_e = (v_o/|u_o|)(1 + D/f_e). [1]
(ii) Objective: 1/v_o = 1/1.25 + 1/(−1.5) = 0.8 − 0.667 = 0.133 → v_o = 7.5 cm; m_o = 7.5/1.5 = 5 (inverted). m_e = 1 + 25/5 = 6 → M = 30. [1]
Eyepiece: 1/u_e = 1/(−25) − 1/5 = −6/25 → u_e = −4.17 cm. Separation = 7.5 + 4.17 ≈ 11.7 cm. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the electric potential at a point at distance r from the centre of a short electric dipole, along a line making angle θ with the dipole axis. Hence show that the potential is zero everywhere on the equatorial line. [3m]
(ii) Charges of +3 nC and −3 nC are 4 mm apart. Find the potential at a point 20 cm from the centre of the dipole on its axis (on the side of the positive charge). How much work is needed to move a small charge along the equatorial line? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Distances of P from +q and −q: r₁ ≈ r − a cos θ, r₂ ≈ r + a cos θ (for r much greater than a). [1]
V = kq(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = kq(2a cos θ)/(r² − a² cos²θ) ≈ kp cos θ/r², where p = 2aq. [1]
On the equatorial line θ = 90°, cos θ = 0 → V = 0 at every point. [1]
(ii) p = 3×10⁻⁹ × 4×10⁻³ = 1.2×10⁻¹¹ C m; V = kp/r² = 9×10⁹ × 1.2×10⁻¹¹/(0.2)² = 2.7 V. [1]
The equatorial line is an equipotential (V = 0), so no work is needed. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State Kirchhoff's two rules. Use them to obtain the condition for balance of a Wheatstone bridge. [3m]
(ii) In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 4 Ω, Q = 8 Ω and R = 6 Ω, and the fourth arm contains a coil of resistance 36 Ω. What resistance must be connected in parallel with the coil to balance the bridge? [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Junction rule: the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it (charge conservation). Loop rule: the algebraic sum of the potential changes around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). [1]
Bridge ABCD with P in AB, Q in BC, R in AD, S in DC and galvanometer G between B and D. At balance I_g = 0, so the current I₁ in P also flows in Q and I₂ in R also flows in S. [1]
Loop ABDA: I₁P − I₂R = 0; loop BCDB: I₁Q − I₂S = 0. Dividing: P/Q = R/S. [1]
(ii) Required S = QR/P = 8 × 6/4 = 12 Ω. [1]
36x/(36 + x) = 12 → 24x = 432 → x = 18 Ω in parallel with the coil. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Define mutual inductance. Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length l, the inner one of radius r₁ with n₁ turns per unit length and the outer one with n₂ turns per unit length. [3m]
(ii) Two coaxial solenoids are each 0.5 m long. The inner one has radius 1 cm and 400 turns; the outer one has 1000 turns. Find their mutual inductance and the emf induced in the inner solenoid when the current in the outer one changes at 50 A/s. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Mutual inductance M: flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other (N₂φ₂ = M I₁); equivalently, emf induced in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other. [1]
Current I₂ in the outer solenoid gives a uniform field B = μ₀n₂I₂ inside it. Flux linkage with the inner solenoid = (n₁l)(πr₁²)(μ₀n₂I₂). [1]
M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l (the same value is obtained by taking current in the inner coil). [1]
(ii) n₁ = 800 m⁻¹, n₂ = 2000 m⁻¹: M = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 800 × 2000 × π(0.01)² × 0.5 ≈ 3.16×10⁻⁴ H. [1]
|e| = M dI/dt = 3.16×10⁻⁴ × 50 ≈ 1.58×10⁻² V ≈ 15.8 mV. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) An alternating voltage v = v₀ sin ωt is applied across a pure capacitor C. Obtain the expression for the current and show that it leads the voltage by π/2. Show that the average power over a cycle is zero. [3m]
(ii) A 50 μF capacitor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find its reactance and the rms and peak values of the current. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) q = Cv = Cv₀ sin ωt → i = dq/dt = ωCv₀ cos ωt = i₀ sin(ωt + π/2), with i₀ = v₀/X_C and X_C = 1/(ωC). [1]
So the current reaches its maximum a quarter cycle before the voltage: it leads by π/2. [1]
P_av = V_rms I_rms cos(π/2) = 0 (the capacitor stores energy for a quarter cycle and returns it in the next). [1]
(ii) X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 50×10⁻⁶) ≈ 63.7 Ω. [1]
I_rms = 220/63.7 ≈ 3.46 A; I₀ = √2 × 3.46 ≈ 4.89 A. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) With a labelled diagram, describe a Cassegrain reflecting telescope. Give two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope. [3m]
(ii) The objective mirror of a reflecting telescope has a radius of curvature of 4 m and the eyepiece has a focal length of 2 cm. Find the magnifying power in normal adjustment. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Diagram: a large concave (paraboloidal) primary mirror with a hole at its centre; a small convex secondary mirror placed before the primary's focus reflects the converging rays back through the hole to form the image, which is viewed with an eyepiece behind the primary. [2]
Advantages (any two): no chromatic aberration (reflection does not depend on wavelength); paraboloidal mirror removes spherical aberration; a mirror needs support only at its back, so very large apertures are possible (more light, better resolution); cheaper to make a large mirror than a large lens. [1]
(ii) f₀ = R/2 = 2 m = 200 cm; m = f₀/f_e = 200/2 = 100. [2]
items.orq:
(B) (i) What are coherent sources? Two coherent waves of equal amplitude a, with phase difference φ, superpose at a point. Show that the resultant intensity is I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2), where I₀ is the intensity of each wave, and write the conditions for constructive and destructive interference. [3m]
(ii) In a Young's double-slit experiment the intensity at the central maximum is I_max. Find the intensity at points where the path difference is (a) λ/4, (b) λ/3. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a constant (time-independent) phase difference. [½]
y₁ = a cos ωt, y₂ = a cos(ωt + φ) → y = 2a cos(φ/2) cos(ωt + φ/2); resultant amplitude 2a cos(φ/2). [1]
Intensity ∝ amplitude²: I = 4a² cos²(φ/2) = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2). [½]
Constructive: φ = 2nπ (path difference nλ) → I = 4I₀; destructive: φ = (2n + 1)π (path difference (n + ½)λ) → I = 0. [1]
(ii) I_max = 4I₀, so I = I_max cos²(φ/2) with φ = (2π/λ) × path difference. [½]
(a) φ = π/2 → I = I_max cos²45° = I_max/2. [½]
(b) φ = 2π/3 → I = I_max cos²60° = I_max/4. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor. Hence show that the energy density of the electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is ½ε₀E². [3m]
(ii) A parallel plate air capacitor has plates of area 0.04 m² separated by 2 mm and is connected to a 100 V supply. Find its capacitance, the energy stored and the energy density between the plates. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) To transfer charge dq when the capacitor already has charge q (p.d. q/C), work dW = (q/C)dq. W = ∫₀^Q (q/C)dq = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV, stored as electric potential energy. [1½]
For a parallel plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d and V = Ed: U = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)² = ½ε₀E²(Ad). Since Ad is the volume between the plates, energy density u = ½ε₀E². [1½]
(ii) C = ε₀A/d = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.04/0.002 = 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ F = 177 pF; U = ½CV² = ½ × 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ × 100² ≈ 8.85×10⁻⁷ J. [1]
E = V/d = 5×10⁴ V/m; u = ½ × 8.85×10⁻¹² × (5×10⁴)² ≈ 1.1×10⁻² J/m³ (check: u × volume = 0.011 × 8×10⁻⁵ ≈ 8.85×10⁻⁷ J). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Derive an expression for the torque on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field. Hence obtain the expression for the potential energy of the dipole, U = −pE cos θ. [3m]
(ii) An electric dipole of moment 2×10⁻⁸ C m is in a uniform field of 5×10⁴ N/C. Find the torque when its axis is perpendicular to the field, and the work done in turning it from the position of stable equilibrium to that of unstable equilibrium. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Forces +qE and −qE act on the charges (separation 2a): net force zero, but they form a couple. Perpendicular distance between the lines of action = 2a sin θ, so τ = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ, i.e. τ = p × E. [1½]
Work done in rotating the dipole from θ₀ to θ: W = ∫pE sin θ dθ = pE(cos θ₀ − cos θ). Taking U = 0 at θ₀ = 90°: U(θ) = −pE cos θ = −p·E. [1½]
(ii) τ = pE sin 90° = 2×10⁻⁸ × 5×10⁴ = 1×10⁻³ N m. [1]
Stable (θ = 0°) to unstable (θ = 180°): W = pE(cos 0° − cos 180°) = 2pE = 2×10⁻³ J. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Explain the principle and working of a moving-coil galvanometer. Why is the magnetic field made radial, and why is a soft-iron core used? Define its current sensitivity. [3m]
(ii) A galvanometer coil has 100 turns, each of area 2 cm², and hangs in a radial field of 0.25 T. The torsional constant of the suspension is 1×10⁻⁶ N m per degree. Find the deflection for a current of 1 mA and the current sensitivity. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Principle: a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque τ = NIAB. The coil turns until this is balanced by the restoring torque kφ of the spring: NIAB = kφ → φ = (NAB/k)I, so deflection ∝ current. [1]
The concave pole pieces and the soft-iron cylindrical core make the field radial and stronger, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B (sin 90° = 1) and the scale is linear; the core also increases the field (and sensitivity). [1]
Current sensitivity = φ/I = NAB/k (deflection per unit current). [1]
(ii) τ = NIAB = 100 × 1×10⁻³ × 2×10⁻⁴ × 0.25 = 5×10⁻⁶ N m; φ = τ/k = 5×10⁻⁶/1×10⁻⁶ = 5°. [1]
Current sensitivity = 5° per mA (5×10³ degree per ampere). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Obtain an expression for the average power dissipated in a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source. Define power factor and explain the term wattless current. [3m]
(ii) In an AC circuit the rms voltage is 220 V and the rms current is 5 A, the current lagging the voltage by 60°. Find the average power consumed and the wattless component of the current. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) v = v₀ sin ωt, i = i₀ sin(ωt − φ). Instantaneous power p = vi = v₀i₀ sin ωt sin(ωt − φ) = (v₀i₀/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so P_av = (v₀i₀/2) cos φ = V_rms I_rms cos φ. [1½]
Power factor = cos φ = R/Z. [½]
Wattless current: the component of current I_rms sin φ, perpendicular (90° out of phase) to the voltage; it contributes zero average power. [1]
(ii) P = 220 × 5 × cos 60° = 550 W. [1]
Wattless component = I_rms sin 60° = 5 × 0.866 ≈ 4.33 A. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) A spherical surface of radius of curvature R separates a rarer medium (refractive index μ₁) from a denser medium (μ₂). Derive the relation μ₂/v − μ₁/u = (μ₂ − μ₁)/R for a point object on the principal axis in the rarer medium (real image in the denser medium). [3m]
(ii) One end of a long glass rod (μ = 1.5) is ground into a convex hemispherical surface of radius 6 cm. An object is placed in air on the axis, 30 cm from this surface. Find the position of the image. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Ray from O strikes the surface at N and refracts towards the normal NC to meet the axis at I. For small angles: i = α + γ, r = γ − β, with α ≈ MN/OM, β ≈ MN/MI, γ ≈ MN/MC. [1]
Snell's law for small angles: μ₁i = μ₂r → μ₁(α + γ) = μ₂(γ − β). [1]
Substituting: μ₁/OM + μ₂/MI = (μ₂ − μ₁)/MC. With the sign convention OM = −u, MI = +v, MC = +R: μ₂/v − μ₁/u = (μ₂ − μ₁)/R. [1]
(ii) μ₁ = 1, μ₂ = 1.5, u = −30 cm, R = +6 cm: 1.5/v = 0.5/6 + 1/(−30) = 0.0833 − 0.0333 = 0.05. [1]
v = 1.5/0.05 = +30 cm: a real image forms inside the rod, 30 cm from the surface. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Draw the graph of angle of deviation δ against angle of incidence i for a prism. Derive the relation μ = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2), where δ_m is the angle of minimum deviation. [3m]
(ii) A ray passes through a prism of angle 60° and refractive index 1.6 in the position of minimum deviation. Find the angle of incidence and the angle of minimum deviation. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Graph: δ first decreases as i increases, reaches a minimum δ_m, then increases (U-shaped curve); for every δ other than δ_m there are two values of i. [1]
For any ray: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A. At minimum deviation i = e and r₁ = r₂ = r, so r = A/2 and i = (A + δ_m)/2. [1]
μ = sin i/sin r = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2). [1]
(ii) r = 30°; sin i = 1.6 × sin 30° = 0.8 → i ≈ 53.1°. [1]
δ_m = 2i − A = 106.3° − 60° ≈ 46.3°. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole, at distance r from its centre. Show that for r much greater than a, E = kp/r³, and state its direction. [3m]
(ii) Charges of +2 nC and −2 nC are 4 mm apart. Find the electric field at a point 15 cm from the centre on the equatorial line, and the force on a charge of 1 μC placed there. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Charges +q at B and −q at A, separation 2a; P on the perpendicular bisector at distance r. Each charge is at distance √(r² + a²) from P and gives a field of magnitude kq/(r² + a²). [1]
The components perpendicular to the axis cancel; the components parallel to the axis add (both point from +q towards −q): E = 2 × kq/(r² + a²) × a/√(r² + a²) = k(2aq)/(r² + a²)^(3/2) = kp/(r² + a²)^(3/2). [1]
For r much greater than a: E = kp/r³, directed opposite to the dipole moment p (from + towards −, parallel to the axis). [1]
(ii) p = 2×10⁻⁹ × 4×10⁻³ = 8×10⁻¹² C m; E = kp/r³ = 9×10⁹ × 8×10⁻¹²/(0.15)³ ≈ 21.3 N/C, antiparallel to p. [1]
F = qE = 1×10⁻⁶ × 21.3 ≈ 2.1×10⁻⁵ N, along the field. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Define the emf and internal resistance of a cell. Obtain the relation between emf E, terminal potential difference V and internal resistance r when the cell (a) supplies a current I to an external resistor, (b) is being charged by a current I. [3m]
(ii) A 12 V battery of internal resistance 0.4 Ω is charged from a 15 V DC supply through a series resistor of 2.6 Ω. Find the charging current and the terminal voltage of the battery during charging. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Emf: the potential difference between the terminals when no current is drawn (work done per unit charge by the source in taking charge round the complete circuit). Internal resistance r: the resistance offered by the electrolyte/material inside the cell to the flow of current. [1]
(a) Discharging: E = I(R + r) and V = IR, so V = E − Ir (V is less than E). [1]
(b) Charging: the external source drives current into the positive terminal against the emf, so it must supply E plus the drop in r: V = E + Ir (V is greater than E). [1]
(ii) Net emf driving the current = 15 − 12 = 3 V; total resistance = 2.6 + 0.4 = 3 Ω; I = 3/3 = 1 A. [1]
Terminal voltage of battery = E + Ir = 12 + 1 × 0.4 = 12.4 V. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Obtain an expression for the self-inductance of a long air-cored solenoid of length l, cross-sectional area A and n turns per unit length. Show that the energy stored in an inductor carrying current I is ½LI². [3m]
(ii) A solenoid 50 cm long has 500 turns and a cross-sectional area of 4 cm². Find its self-inductance and the magnetic energy stored when it carries a current of 3 A. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Field inside: B = μ₀nI. Total turns N = nl; flux linkage Nφ = (nl)(μ₀nI)A = μ₀n²AlI. Since Nφ = LI, L = μ₀n²Al. [1½]
While the current grows, the back emf e = L dI/dt opposes it; work done by the source in time dt: dW = eI dt = LI dI. Total work W = ∫₀^I LI dI = ½LI², stored as magnetic energy. [1½]
(ii) n = 500/0.5 = 1000 m⁻¹; L = 4π×10⁻⁷ × (1000)² × 4×10⁻⁴ × 0.5 ≈ 2.51×10⁻⁴ H. [1]
U = ½LI² = ½ × 2.51×10⁻⁴ × 3² ≈ 1.13×10⁻³ J. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) For a series LCR circuit connected to a source of variable frequency, obtain the condition for resonance and the resonant frequency. Sketch (describe) how the current varies with frequency for two different values of R, and define the quality factor. [3m]
(ii) The tuning circuit of a medium-wave radio receiver has an inductance of 0.5 mH, a capacitance of 200 pF and a resistance of 10 Ω. Find the resonant frequency and the quality factor. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) I = V/√[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]. I is maximum (Z minimum = R) when X_L = X_C, i.e. ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C) → ω₀ = 1/√(LC), ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). [1½]
Graph: current rises to a peak V/R at ω₀ and falls on either side; for smaller R the peak is higher and sharper, for larger R it is lower and broader. [½]
Quality factor Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR) = ω₀/(2Δω), a measure of the sharpness of resonance. [1]
(ii) ω₀ = 1/√(0.5×10⁻³ × 200×10⁻¹²) = 1/√(10⁻¹³) ≈ 3.16×10⁶ rad/s; ν₀ = ω₀/2π ≈ 5.03×10⁵ Hz ≈ 503 kHz. [1]
Q = ω₀L/R = 3.16×10⁶ × 0.5×10⁻³/10 ≈ 158. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Two thin lenses of focal lengths f₁ and f₂ are placed in contact. Derive an expression for the focal length of the combination, and write the relations for the power and the magnification of the combination. [3m]
(ii) A convex lens of power +5 D is placed in contact with another lens, and the combination behaves as a lens of focal length −40 cm. Find the focal length and nature of the second lens. Where will the combination form the image of an object placed 60 cm in front of it? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Object O at distance u from the first lens: 1/v₁ − 1/u = 1/f₁. The image I₁ acts as the object for the second lens (in contact, so same distance v₁): 1/v − 1/v₁ = 1/f₂. [1]
Adding: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. For a single equivalent lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/F, so 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. [1]
Power: P = P₁ + P₂; magnification: m = m₁ × m₂. [1]
(ii) P = 100/(−40) = −2.5 D. P₂ = P − P₁ = −2.5 − 5 = −7.5 D → f₂ = 100/(−7.5) ≈ −13.3 cm: a concave (diverging) lens. [1]
1/v = 1/F + 1/u = −1/40 − 1/60 = −1/24 → v = −24 cm: a virtual, erect, diminished image (m = 0.4) 24 cm in front of the combination. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State Huygens' principle. Using it, prove the law of reflection for a plane wavefront incident on a plane reflecting surface. [3m]
(ii) Draw (describe) the shape of the wavefront that emerges when a plane wavefront (a) passes through a thin prism, (b) passes through a thin convex lens, (c) is reflected by a concave mirror. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Each point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets spreading with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets. [1]
Plane wavefront AB meets the mirror MN at A at angle i. While the wavelet from B travels BC = vt to the surface, the wavelet from A spreads to radius AE = vt. The tangent CE is the reflected wavefront. [1]
Triangles EAC and BCA are congruent (common hypotenuse AC, right angles at E and B, AE = BC = vt), so ∠BAC = ∠ECA, i.e. angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r. [1]
(ii) (a) A plane wavefront, tilted (the part passing through the thicker part of the prism is delayed more). [½]
(b) A spherical wavefront converging to the focus (the thicker central part delays the middle of the wavefront). [½]
(c) A spherical wavefront converging to the focus of the mirror. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Derive an expression for the electric potential at a distance r from a point charge q. Show (describe) graphically how the potential and the electric field due to the charge vary with r. [3m]
(ii) Charges of +5 μC and −2 μC are held 6 cm apart in air. Find the electrostatic potential energy of the system and the work needed to increase their separation to 12 cm. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Potential at P = work done per unit charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to P against the field. At distance x the force on a unit positive charge is kq/x² (outward), so the external force is −kq/x². [1]
V = −∫_∞^r (kq/x²) dx = kq/r = q/(4πε₀r). [1]
Graph: V ∝ 1/r (falls gradually), E ∝ 1/r² (falls more steeply); both tend to zero as r → ∞. [1]
(ii) U = kq₁q₂/r = 9×10⁹ × (5×10⁻⁶)(−2×10⁻⁶)/0.06 = −1.5 J. [1]
At 12 cm U′ = −0.75 J; work needed W = U′ − U = −0.75 − (−1.5) = +0.75 J. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Derive expressions for the equivalent capacitance of capacitors C₁, C₂, C₃ connected (a) in series, (b) in parallel. [3m]
(ii) Capacitors of 2 μF and 3 μF are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 5 μF capacitor across a 100 V supply. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge on the 5 μF capacitor and the charge on the 2 μF capacitor. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) (a) Series: each capacitor carries the same charge Q, and V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ + Q/C₃. With V = Q/C: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃. [1½]
(b) Parallel: each has the same p.d. V, and Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃ = (C₁ + C₂ + C₃)V. With Q = CV: C = C₁ + C₂ + C₃. [1½]
(ii) Parallel part = 2 + 3 = 5 μF; in series with 5 μF: C = 5 × 5/(5 + 5) = 2.5 μF. Charge on the 5 μF capacitor Q = CV = 2.5 × 100 = 250 μC. [1]
The parallel group also carries 250 μC on 5 μF, so its p.d. = 50 V; charge on 2 μF = 2 × 50 = 100 μC (and 150 μC on 3 μF). [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Using Ampere's circuital law, obtain an expression for the magnetic field inside a toroid of N turns and mean radius r carrying current I. Show that the field is zero in the open space inside the toroid and outside it. [3m]
(ii) A toroid of mean radius 15 cm has 3000 turns and carries a current of 0.5 A. Its core is made of a ferromagnetic material of relative permeability 500. Find the magnetic intensity H and the magnetic field B in the core. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Inside the core: take a circular Amperian loop of radius r along the core. B is tangential and constant on it; the loop links N turns, so enclosed current = NI: B(2πr) = μ₀NI → B = μ₀NI/(2πr) = μ₀nI, where n = N/(2πr). [1½]
Open space inside: a loop there encloses no current → B = 0. [½]
Outside: a loop outside is threaded by each turn twice, in opposite directions (current going in and coming out), so the net enclosed current is zero → B = 0. [1]
(ii) H = NI/(2πr) = 3000 × 0.5/(2π × 0.15) ≈ 1.59×10³ A/m. [1]
B = μ₀μᵣH = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 500 × 1.59×10³ ≈ 1.0 T. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) An alternating current i = i₀ sin ωt flows through a resistor R. Show that the rms value of the current is i₀/√2 and that the average power is I_rms²R. Draw the phasor diagram for a pure resistor. [3m]
(ii) A voltage v = 200 sin 314t volt is applied across a 100 Ω resistor. Find the frequency of the supply, the rms current and the average power dissipated. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) p = i²R = i₀²R sin²ωt. The average of sin²ωt over a complete cycle is ½ (since sin²ωt = (1 − cos 2ωt)/2 and cos 2ωt averages to zero), so P_av = ½i₀²R. [1½]
Defining the rms current by P_av = I_rms²R: I_rms² = i₀²/2 → I_rms = i₀/√2 ≈ 0.707 i₀. [1]
Phasor diagram: the V and I phasors lie along the same line (zero phase difference), rotating together at ω. [½]
(ii) ω = 314 rad/s → ν = 314/2π ≈ 50 Hz. i₀ = 200/100 = 2 A, I_rms = 2/√2 ≈ 1.41 A. [1]
P = I_rms²R = 2 × 100 = 200 W. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Draw a ray diagram for a convex lens forming a real image of an object placed beyond 2F, and use it to derive the thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Also write the expression for linear magnification. [3m]
(ii) An object 1.5 cm tall is placed 12 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 18 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Ray parallel to the axis refracts through F; ray through the optical centre O goes undeviated; they meet at the real, inverted image A′B′. [1]
ΔABO ~ ΔA′B′O: A′B′/AB = OB′/OB. ΔOMF ~ ΔB′A′F (MO = AB): A′B′/AB = FB′/OF = (OB′ − OF)/OF. [1]
So OB′/OB = (OB′ − OF)/OF. With OB = −u, OB′ = +v, OF = +f: v/(−u) = (v − f)/f → vf = −uv + uf; dividing by uvf: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h′/h = v/u. [1]
(ii) 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/18 − 1/12 = −1/36 → v = −36 cm: the image is 36 cm from the lens, on the same side as the object. [1]
m = v/u = (−36)/(−12) = +3 → h′ = 4.5 cm; virtual, erect and magnified (the lens acts as a magnifier). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) For the refraction of a ray through a prism, show that i + e = A + δ. Hence show that for a thin prism (small angle A) the deviation is δ = (μ − 1)A, independent of the angle of incidence (for small i). [3m]
(ii) A thin prism of angle 6° and refractive index 1.5 is combined with another thin prism of refractive index 1.75 so that the combination produces no deviation of a ray. Find the angle of the second prism and how it must be placed. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) In the quadrilateral formed by the two faces and the two normals, the angle between the normals is 180° − A, so r₁ + r₂ = A. Deviation δ = (i − r₁) + (e − r₂) = i + e − A, i.e. i + e = A + δ. [1½]
For a thin prism and small i, all angles are small: i = μr₁ and e = μr₂, so δ = μ(r₁ + r₂) − A = μA − A = (μ − 1)A. [1½]
(ii) δ₁ = (1.5 − 1) × 6° = 3°. For zero net deviation, δ₂ = (1.75 − 1)A₂ = 3° → A₂ = 4°. [1]
The second prism must be placed inverted with respect to the first (its apex on the side of the first prism's base), so that its deviation is opposite. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Two cells of emfs E₁, E₂ and internal resistances r₁, r₂ are connected (a) in series, (b) in parallel (positive terminals joined together). Derive the expressions for the equivalent emf and equivalent internal resistance in each case. [3m]
(ii) Cells of 1.5 V (internal resistance 0.3 Ω) and 2.0 V (internal resistance 0.2 Ω) are joined in series and connected to a 2 Ω resistor. Find the current and the terminal voltage of each cell. What current would flow if the 2 Ω resistor were replaced by a thick wire of negligible resistance? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) (a) Series (+ of one to − of the other): V_AC = V_AB + V_BC = (E₁ − Ir₁) + (E₂ − Ir₂) = (E₁ + E₂) − I(r₁ + r₂). Comparing with V = E_eq − I r_eq: E_eq = E₁ + E₂, r_eq = r₁ + r₂. [1]
(b) Parallel: both cells have the same terminal p.d. V. I₁ = (E₁ − V)/r₁, I₂ = (E₂ − V)/r₂, and I = I₁ + I₂ = E₁/r₁ + E₂/r₂ − V(1/r₁ + 1/r₂). [1]
So V = (E₁r₂ + E₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) − I r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂), giving E_eq = (E₁r₂ + E₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂). [1]
(ii) I = (1.5 + 2.0)/(2 + 0.3 + 0.2) = 3.5/2.5 = 1.4 A. V₁ = 1.5 − 1.4 × 0.3 = 1.08 V; V₂ = 2.0 − 1.4 × 0.2 = 1.72 V. [1]
With the resistor replaced by a thick wire, only the internal resistances limit the current: I = 3.5/(0.3 + 0.2) = 7 A. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Show that, in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is σ/ε₀ and is normal to the surface. Explain why any excess charge resides on the outer surface, and what is meant by electrostatic shielding. [3m]
(ii) An isolated conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 4.0 nC. Find the surface charge density, the electric field just outside its surface, and the potential at its centre. (k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻², ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Inside the conductor E = 0 (else free charges would move). A tangential component at the surface would also move charges, so E must be normal to the surface. [1]
Take a small pill-box of face area ΔS across the surface: flux only through the outer face = EΔS; charge enclosed = σΔS. Gauss's law: EΔS = σΔS/ε₀ → E = σ/ε₀ (along the outward normal for σ > 0). [1]
A Gaussian surface just inside the conductor has E = 0, so it encloses no net charge — the excess charge lies on the outer surface. The field inside a cavity in a conductor (with no charge in it) is zero whatever the outside field, so sensitive instruments placed inside a metal enclosure are shielded. [1]
(ii) σ = Q/4πR² = 4.0×10⁻⁹/(4π × 0.01) ≈ 3.2×10⁻⁸ C/m²; E = kQ/R² = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁹/0.01 = 3600 N/C (= σ/ε₀). [1]
Potential is the same throughout the conductor: V = kQ/R = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁹/0.1 = 360 V at the centre (where E = 0). [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) A rectangular loop of sides a and b, carrying a current I, is placed in a uniform magnetic field B, with the normal to its plane making an angle θ with B. Derive an expression for the torque on the loop and write it in vector form in terms of the magnetic moment. [3m]
(ii) A square coil of side 10 cm with 20 turns carries a current of 0.5 A and hangs in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. Find the torque on it when its plane is (a) parallel to the field, (b) perpendicular to the field. In which position is it in stable equilibrium? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) The forces on the two sides of length b (parallel to the axis of rotation) are each IbB, equal and opposite and along different lines; the forces on the sides of length a cancel and are collinear. [1]
The perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces IbB is a sin θ, so τ = IbB × a sin θ = IAB sin θ (A = ab). For N turns τ = NIAB sin θ. [1]
With magnetic moment m = NIA (direction along the normal by the right-hand rule): τ = m × B. [1]
(ii) m = NIA = 20 × 0.5 × 0.01 = 0.1 A m². (a) Plane parallel to B → normal ⊥ B, θ = 90°: τ = mB = 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02 N m (maximum). [1]
(b) Plane perpendicular to B → θ = 0 (or 180°): τ = 0. Stable equilibrium is when m is along B (θ = 0); with m opposite to B it is unstable. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) A conducting rod of length l slides with constant velocity v on two parallel conducting rails joined by a resistor R, in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Derive expressions for the induced emf, the induced current and the force needed to keep the rod moving, and show that the mechanical power supplied equals the electrical power dissipated in R. [3m]
(ii) In such an arrangement l = 0.40 m, B = 0.25 T, R = 2 Ω and v = 5 m/s (rails and rod of negligible resistance). Find the current, the force needed, and the power dissipated. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Flux through the circuit Φ = Blx, where x is the length of the circuit; dx/dt = v, so |e| = dΦ/dt = Blv (equally, the Lorentz force qvB on the charges in the rod). [1]
Current I = Blv/R. The rod carrying I in B feels a force IlB opposing the motion (Lenz's law), so an equal external force F = IlB = B²l²v/R is needed for constant velocity. [1]
Mechanical power P = Fv = B²l²v²/R; electrical power I²R = (Blv/R)²R = B²l²v²/R — the same, so the work done by the agent appears as Joule heat (energy conservation). [1]
(ii) e = Blv = 0.25 × 0.40 × 5 = 0.5 V; I = 0.5/2 = 0.25 A. [1]
F = IlB = 0.25 × 0.40 × 0.25 = 0.025 N; P = Fv = 0.125 W (= I²R = 0.0625 × 2). [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) What is a simple microscope? Derive expressions for its magnifying power when the final image is formed (a) at the near point (least distance of distinct vision D), (b) at infinity. [3m]
(ii) A watch repairer uses a convex lens of power +12.5 D as a magnifier. Find the magnifying power when the image is (a) at 25 cm, (b) at infinity, and the distance at which the object must be held in case (a). [2m]
items.ans:
(i) A simple microscope is a converging lens held close to the eye, with the object placed within its focal length so that a virtual, erect, enlarged image is formed. [½]
(a) Image at D: v = −D. From 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, the magnification m = v/u = 1 − v/f = 1 + D/f. With the eye close to the lens, the angular magnification equals this m, so M = 1 + D/f. [1½]
(b) Image at infinity: object at the focus. The angle subtended by the image is θ = h/f, while the object at D subtends θ₀ = h/D, so M = θ/θ₀ = D/f. [1]
(ii) f = 1/12.5 m = 8 cm. (a) M = 1 + 25/8 ≈ 4.1; (b) M = 25/8 ≈ 3.1. [1]
For (a): v = −25 cm, 1/u = 1/v − 1/f = −1/25 − 1/8 = −0.165 → u ≈ −6.1 cm, i.e. about 6.1 cm from the lens. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) What is total internal reflection? State the two conditions for it. Using Snell's law, obtain the relation between the critical angle C and the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer medium. Explain briefly how an optical fibre uses total internal reflection. [3m]
(ii) A ray travels inside a glass block (μ = 1.5) towards its plane face, which is in contact with a transparent liquid. Total internal reflection is found to occur only when the angle of incidence exceeds 60°. Find the refractive index of the liquid. Can total internal reflection occur if the liquid is replaced by one of refractive index 1.6? [2m]
items.orans:
(i) When light travelling in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, no light is refracted; it is all reflected back — total internal reflection. Conditions: light must go from the optically denser to the rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. [1]
At i = C the refraction angle is 90°: μ₁ sin C = μ₂ sin 90° → sin C = μ₂/μ₁ = 1/μ₁₂ (= 1/μ for a medium in air). [1]
An optical fibre has a core of higher refractive index surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering at a small angle strikes the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle and is totally reflected again and again, so it travels along the (even bent) fibre with very little loss. [1]
(ii) sin C = μ_l/μ_g → μ_l = 1.5 × sin 60° = 1.5 × 0.866 ≈ 1.30. [1]
No: a liquid of μ = 1.6 is optically denser than the glass, and total internal reflection can occur only when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Explain, with a diagram, what happens to a dielectric slab placed in a uniform external electric field E₀ (polarisation). Show that the field inside the slab is reduced to E₀/K and hence that the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor becomes K times when the space between its plates is completely filled with the dielectric. [3m]
(ii) A 400 pF capacitor is charged to 150 V and disconnected from the battery. It is then connected across an uncharged 200 pF capacitor. Find the common potential and the energy lost in the process. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) In the field, the molecules of the dielectric become polarised (non-polar molecules develop induced dipoles; polar molecules partly align), giving a dipole moment per unit volume P along E₀. Inside, the charges cancel, but a surface charge −σ_p appears on the face near the positive plate and +σ_p on the other face. [1]
These induced charges set up a field opposite to E₀, so the net field inside is E = E₀ − σ_p/ε₀ = E₀/K, where K (the dielectric constant) > 1. [1]
For a capacitor with charge Q fixed: V = Ed = E₀d/K = V₀/K, so C = Q/V = K(Q/V₀) = KC₀ = Kε₀A/d. [1]
(ii) Charge is conserved: V = C₁V₁/(C₁ + C₂) = (400 × 150)/600 = 100 V. [1]
U_i = ½ × 400×10⁻¹² × 150² = 4.5×10⁻⁶ J; U_f = ½ × 600×10⁻¹² × 100² = 3.0×10⁻⁶ J; energy lost = 1.5×10⁻⁶ J (as heat and electromagnetic radiation in the connecting wires). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State Gauss's law in electrostatics. Use it to obtain the electric field due to an isolated point charge q, and hence deduce Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges. [3m]
(ii) A spherical Gaussian surface of radius 10 cm encloses charges of +3 μC and −5 μC, while a charge of +4 μC lies outside it. Find the net electric flux through the surface. Would the flux change if the radius of the surface were doubled (still not enclosing the +4 μC charge)? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface is 1/ε₀ times the net charge enclosed, ∮E·dS = q_enc/ε₀. [1]
Take a sphere of radius r centred on q. By symmetry E is radial and has the same magnitude everywhere on it: E × 4πr² = q/ε₀ → E = q/(4πε₀r²). [1]
A second charge q₀ at distance r experiences F = q₀E = qq₀/(4πε₀r²), along the line joining them — Coulomb's law. [1]
(ii) Φ = q_enc/ε₀ = (3 − 5)×10⁻⁶/8.85×10⁻¹² ≈ −2.26×10⁵ N m² C⁻¹ (net flux inward). The outside charge contributes no net flux. [1]
No — the flux depends only on the charge enclosed, not on the size of the surface. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Starting from the Lorentz force on a moving charge, derive an expression for the force on a straight conductor of length l carrying a current I in a uniform magnetic field B, in vector form. [3m]
(ii) A straight wire 20 cm long carries a current of 3 A along the +x direction in a uniform magnetic field B = (0.4 î + 0.3 ĵ) T. Find the force on the wire (magnitude and direction). Which component of the field exerts no force? [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Each free electron moving with drift velocity v_d experiences F = q(v_d × B) = −e(v_d × B). [1]
The conductor has n electrons per unit volume, so the number in length l is nAl and the total force F = −nAl e (v_d × B). [1]
Since the current I = neAv_d flows opposite to v_d, writing l as a vector along the current: F = I(l × B), of magnitude IlB sin θ. [1]
(ii) F = I(l × B) = 3 × 0.2 î × (0.4 î + 0.3 ĵ) = 0.6 × 0.3 (î × ĵ) = 0.18 k̂ N. [1]
So F = 0.18 N along +z. The 0.4 î T component is parallel to the current (î × î = 0), so it exerts no force. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and Lenz's law. Show, with the example of a bar magnet pushed towards a closed coil, that Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy. [3m]
(ii) A square loop of side 10 cm and resistance 0.5 Ω lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.8 T confined to a region with a straight edge. The loop is pulled out of the field at a steady 2 cm/s, keeping one side parallel to the edge. Find the induced emf, the induced current, the time for which it flows, and the heat produced in the loop. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Faraday's law: the magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through it, e = −N dΦ/dt. Lenz's law: the induced current flows in such a direction as to oppose the change in flux that produces it (the minus sign). [1]
When the N pole is pushed towards the coil, the induced current makes the near face of the coil a N pole, which repels the magnet; when the magnet is pulled away, the near face becomes an S pole and attracts it. [1]
In both cases work must be done against this opposing force, and it is this mechanical work that appears as electrical energy (heat) in the coil. If the induced current aided the change, the magnet would accelerate by itself and energy would be created from nothing — violating energy conservation. [1]
(ii) e = Blv = 0.8 × 0.10 × 0.02 = 1.6×10⁻³ V; I = e/R = 1.6×10⁻³/0.5 = 3.2×10⁻³ A. [1]
Time t = side/speed = 0.10/0.02 = 5 s; heat H = I²Rt = (3.2×10⁻³)² × 0.5 × 5 ≈ 2.6×10⁻⁵ J. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Draw (describe) a labelled ray diagram of an astronomical refracting telescope when the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision D. Derive the expression for its magnifying power in this case. [3m]
(ii) A telescope has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. Find its magnifying power and the distance between the lenses when the final image is at 25 cm from the eye. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Parallel rays from a distant object, making angle α with the axis, form a real, inverted image h at the focus of the objective. The eyepiece is placed so that this image lies within its focal length, at distance u_e, and gives a virtual, magnified final image at distance D. [1]
α ≈ h/f_o (angle subtended at the objective, ≈ at the eye); angle subtended by the final image at the eye β ≈ h/u_e. M = β/α = f_o/u_e. [1]
From the lens formula for the eyepiece with v = −D: 1/u_e = 1/f_e + 1/D, so M = −(f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D) (negative sign: final image inverted). [1]
(ii) |M| = (120/5)(1 + 5/25) = 24 × 1.2 = 28.8. [1]
u_e = f_e D/(f_e + D) = 5 × 25/30 ≈ 4.17 cm; distance between lenses = f_o + u_e = 120 + 4.17 ≈ 124.2 cm. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Draw (describe) a ray diagram for the image formed by a convex mirror and derive the mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for it, using the Cartesian sign convention. Show that the image of a real object is always virtual and erect. [3m]
(ii) A convex security mirror in a shop has a focal length of 30 cm. Where must a customer stand so that his image is half his size? Where is the image formed? [2m]
items.orans:
(i) A ray from the top A of the object parallel to the axis reflects as if coming from the focus F behind the mirror; a ray striking the pole P reflects symmetrically about the axis. The reflected rays diverge and appear to meet at A′ behind the mirror. [1]
From similar triangles (paraxial rays, M close to P): A′B′/AB = PB′/PB and A′B′/AB = FB′/FP = (PF − PB′)/PF. So PB′/PB = (PF − PB′)/PF. With PB = −u, PB′ = +v, PF = +f: v/(−u) = (f − v)/f → vf = −uf + uv; dividing by uvf gives 1/u + 1/v = 1/f. [1]
For a real object u < 0 and f > 0: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u is always positive, so v > 0 — the image is behind the mirror (virtual); m = −v/u > 0, so it is erect (and v < f, so diminished). [1]
(ii) m = −v/u = ½ → v = −u/2. Then 1/v + 1/u = −2/u + 1/u = −1/u = 1/30 → u = −30 cm: he must stand 30 cm in front of the mirror. [1]
v = +15 cm: a virtual, erect image 15 cm behind the mirror. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Show that the electric field at a point is related to the potential by E = −dV/dr. Hence explain why (a) the electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential surface, and (b) no work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface. [3m]
(ii) In a uniform electric field, equipotential surfaces are parallel planes 2 cm apart, with potentials 10 V, 20 V, 30 V, 40 V and 50 V. Find the magnitude and direction of the electric field, and the work done by an external agent in slowly moving a charge of 3 μC from the 10 V surface to the 50 V surface. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Let a unit positive charge be moved through a small displacement dr along the direction of E. The work done on it by an external agent against the field is −E dr, and this equals the change in potential dV. So dV = −E dr, i.e. E = −dV/dr. The field points in the direction in which the potential decreases fastest. [1]
(a) On an equipotential surface dV = 0 for any small displacement dl along it, so E·dl = 0: E has no component along the surface and must be normal to it. [1]
(b) W = q(V_B − V_A) = 0 for two points on the same equipotential surface, so no work is done; equivalently, the force qE is perpendicular to the displacement. [1]
(ii) E = ΔV/Δd = 10 V/0.02 m = 500 V/m, directed from the 50 V plane towards the 10 V plane (direction of decreasing potential). [1]
W = qΔV = 3×10⁻⁶ × (50 − 10) = 1.2×10⁻⁴ J. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Obtain an expression for the electrostatic potential energy of a system of two point charges q₁ and q₂, at positions r₁ and r₂, placed in an external electric field in which the potentials at these points are V(r₁) and V(r₂). [3m]
(ii) Charges of +4 nC and −2 nC are held 3 cm apart in air, in an external field in which the potentials at their positions are +5000 V and +2000 V respectively. Find the potential energy of the system. (k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Bring q₁ from infinity to r₁ against the external field only: work W₁ = q₁V(r₁). [1]
Bring q₂ from infinity to r₂: work must be done against the external field, q₂V(r₂), and against the field of q₁, kq₁q₂/r₁₂, where r₁₂ is the distance between them. [1]
Total work stored as potential energy: U = q₁V(r₁) + q₂V(r₂) + q₁q₂/(4πε₀r₁₂). [1]
(ii) q₁V(r₁) = 4×10⁻⁹ × 5000 = 2.0×10⁻⁵ J; q₂V(r₂) = −2×10⁻⁹ × 2000 = −4.0×10⁻⁶ J; mutual term = 9×10⁹ × (4×10⁻⁹)(−2×10⁻⁹)/0.03 = −2.4×10⁻⁶ J. [1]
U = 2.0×10⁻⁵ − 4.0×10⁻⁶ − 2.4×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.36×10⁻⁵ J. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) An alternating voltage v = v₀ sin ωt is applied across a pure inductor of inductance L. Obtain the expression for the current, and show that the current lags the voltage by π/2. Draw (describe) the phasor diagram and show that the average power consumed over a cycle is zero. [3m]
(ii) A coil of inductance 0.2 H and negligible resistance is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find its inductive reactance and the rms and peak values of the current. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Kirchhoff's loop rule: v₀ sin ωt = L di/dt → di = (v₀/L) sin ωt dt. Integrating, i = −(v₀/ωL) cos ωt = i₀ sin(ωt − π/2), with i₀ = v₀/ωL; X_L = ωL is the inductive reactance. [1]
The current reaches its maximum a quarter-cycle (π/2) after the voltage, so it lags; in the phasor diagram the current phasor is 90° behind (clockwise from) the voltage phasor, both rotating anticlockwise at ω. [1]
P = vi = −v₀i₀ sin ωt cos ωt = −½v₀i₀ sin 2ωt, whose average over a complete cycle is zero: energy stored in the magnetic field in one quarter-cycle is returned to the source in the next. [1]
(ii) X_L = 2πνL = 2π × 50 × 0.2 ≈ 62.8 Ω. [1]
I_rms = 220/62.8 ≈ 3.5 A; I₀ = √2 × 3.5 ≈ 4.95 A. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) A particle of mass m and charge q enters a uniform magnetic field B with velocity v perpendicular to the field. Show that it moves in a circle, and obtain expressions for the radius of the circle and the time period. Show that the period does not depend on the speed. What is the path if v makes an angle with B? [3m]
(ii) An α-particle (mass 6.64×10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C) with a kinetic energy of 2.0 MeV moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. Find its speed, the radius of its path and its time period. (1 MeV = 1.6×10⁻¹³ J) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) The force F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed; a force of constant magnitude qvB always perpendicular to v produces uniform circular motion. [1]
This force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r → r = mv/(qB). Period T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB), which contains no v: faster particles move in larger circles but take the same time per revolution. [1]
If v makes an angle θ with B, the component v cos θ along B is unchanged while v sin θ gives circular motion, so the path is a helix of radius mv sin θ/(qB) and pitch (v cos θ)T. [1]
(ii) v = √(2K/m) = √(2 × 2.0 × 1.6×10⁻¹³/6.64×10⁻²⁷) ≈ 9.8×10⁶ m/s. [1]
r = mv/(qB) = 6.64×10⁻²⁷ × 9.8×10⁶/(3.2×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5) ≈ 0.41 m; T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π × 6.64×10⁻²⁷/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 2.6×10⁻⁷ s. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) An object lies at the bottom of a denser medium of refractive index μ and is viewed from above, nearly along the normal. With a ray diagram, show that its apparent depth is (real depth)/μ, and hence show that a slab of thickness t raises the image of an object below it by t(1 − 1/μ). [3m]
(ii) A travelling microscope is focused on an ink mark on a table. A glass slab 4.5 cm thick (μ = 1.5) is placed over the mark. By how much must the microscope be raised to focus on the mark again? When the glass is replaced by a 4.5 cm layer of a transparent liquid, the microscope has to be raised by 1.2 cm. Find the refractive index of the liquid. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) A ray from the object O at depth OA = h_real, leaving at a small angle, meets the surface at B at angle of incidence i and refracts away from the normal at angle r. Extended backwards, the refracted ray appears to come from I, with IA = h_app. [1]
Snell's law for light going from the medium into air: μ sin i = sin r. For near-normal viewing, sin i ≈ tan i = AB/h_real and sin r ≈ tan r = AB/h_app, so μ(AB/h_real) = AB/h_app → h_app = h_real/μ. [1]
For a slab of thickness t, the object appears at depth t/μ below the top surface, so its image is raised by the normal shift d = t − t/μ = t(1 − 1/μ). [1]
(ii) d = 4.5(1 − 1/1.5) = 4.5 × 1/3 = 1.5 cm: the microscope is raised by 1.5 cm. [1]
For the liquid: 1.2 = 4.5(1 − 1/μ) → 1/μ = 1 − 0.267 = 0.733 → μ ≈ 1.36. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Draw (describe) a labelled ray diagram of a compound microscope in normal adjustment (final image at infinity). Derive the expression for its magnifying power. Why should both the objective and the eyepiece have short focal lengths? [3m]
(ii) A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm, placed 20 cm apart. The final image is at infinity. Find the distance of the object from the objective and the magnifying power. (D = 25 cm) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image A'B' of the small object AB placed just beyond its focus. The eyepiece is placed so that A'B' lies at its first focal point, so the rays emerge parallel and the final image is at infinity (inverted relative to the object). [1]
Magnification by the objective m_o = h'/h = v_o/u_o ≈ L/f_o, where L (tube length) is the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece. Angular magnification by the eyepiece with the image at infinity m_e = D/f_e. [1]
M = m_o × m_e ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e). Since M increases as f_o and f_e decrease, both lenses should have short focal lengths. [1]
(ii) The intermediate image is at the focus of the eyepiece: v_o = 20 − 2.5 = 17.5 cm. 1/u_o = 1/v_o − 1/f_o = 1/17.5 − 1/1.0 → u_o ≈ −1.06 cm: the object is about 1.06 cm in front of the objective. [1]
m_o = v_o/u_o = 17.5/(−1.06) = −16.5; m_e = D/f_e = 25/2.5 = 10; M = −165 (magnifying power 165, final image inverted). [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Explain how the resistivity of (a) a metal such as copper, (b) an alloy such as nichrome, and (c) a semiconductor such as silicon changes with temperature. Give reasons in terms of ρ = m/(ne²τ), and draw (describe) the ρ–T graphs. [3m]
(ii) The copper winding of an electric motor has a resistance of 2.40 Ω at 25 °C. After the motor has run for an hour, the resistance is 2.82 Ω. Taking the temperature coefficient of resistivity of copper as 3.9×10⁻³ °C⁻¹ (referred to 25 °C), find the temperature of the winding. [2m]
items.ans:
(i)(a) Metal: n is practically constant, but with rising temperature the ions vibrate more, collisions become more frequent and τ decreases, so ρ increases — nearly linearly over a wide range, ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]; the graph rises, curving towards a small non-zero value at low temperature. [1]
(b) Alloy (nichrome, manganin): resistivity is high, and it increases only very slightly with temperature (very small α); the graph is almost flat. That is why such alloys are used for heating elements and standard resistors. [1]
(c) Semiconductor: as T rises, many more electron–hole pairs are generated, so n increases rapidly; this outweighs the decrease in τ, and ρ decreases (negative temperature coefficient); the graph falls steeply with temperature. [1]
(ii) R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − 25)] → 2.82 = 2.40[1 + 3.9×10⁻³(T − 25)]. [1]
T − 25 = (2.82/2.40 − 1)/3.9×10⁻³ = 0.175/0.0039 ≈ 44.9 → T ≈ 70 °C. [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) State Gauss's law. Using it, obtain the electric field (a) between and (b) outside two large, thin, parallel plane sheets carrying uniform surface charge densities +σ and −σ. Hence obtain the expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor. [3m]
(ii) Two large parallel plates 2.0 mm apart in air carry surface charge densities of +8.85×10⁻⁸ C/m² and −8.85×10⁻⁸ C/m². Find the electric field between the plates, the potential difference between them, and the force on an electron placed between them. (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) Gauss's law: ∮E·dS = q_enc/ε₀. For one infinite sheet, take a cylindrical Gaussian surface crossing the sheet with end-faces of area A: flux passes only through the two ends, 2EA = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/2ε₀, normal to the sheet, away from a positive sheet. [1]
(a) Between the sheets, the fields of +σ (away from it) and −σ (towards it) point the same way: E = σ/2ε₀ + σ/2ε₀ = σ/ε₀, from the positive to the negative sheet. (b) Outside, the two fields are equal and opposite: E = 0. [1]
For plates of area A, separation d: V = Ed = σd/ε₀ = Qd/(ε₀A), so C = Q/V = ε₀A/d. [1]
(ii) E = σ/ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻⁸/8.85×10⁻¹² = 1.0×10⁴ V/m; V = Ed = 1.0×10⁴ × 2.0×10⁻³ = 20 V. [1]
F = eE = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0×10⁴ = 1.6×10⁻¹⁵ N, towards the positive plate. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) A metal rod of length l rotates with a constant angular velocity ω about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod, in a uniform magnetic field B parallel to the axis. Derive an expression for the emf induced between the ends of the rod. [3m]
(ii) The metal blades of a ceiling fan in Delhi are 0.60 m long (measured from the axis) and the fan turns at 300 revolutions per minute in a horizontal plane. The vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field there is 0.40×10⁻⁴ T. Find the emf induced between the axis and the tip of a blade. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) Consider an element of length dr at distance r from the axis; its speed is v = ωr, perpendicular to both the rod and B. [1]
The motional emf across it is dε = Bv dr = Bωr dr. [1]
Adding over the whole rod: ε = ∫₀ˡ Bωr dr = ½Bωl². (Equivalently, the rod sweeps area ½l²ω per second, so ε = B × dA/dt.) [1]
(ii) ω = 2π × 300/60 = 10π ≈ 31.4 rad/s. [1]
ε = ½ × 0.40×10⁻⁴ × 31.4 × (0.60)² ≈ 2.3×10⁻⁴ V (about 0.23 mV). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) Write the expression for the Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in an electric field E and a magnetic field B. Show that a charged particle moving perpendicular to mutually perpendicular fields E and B passes through undeflected if v = E/B. Also show that the magnetic force does no work on the particle. [3m]
(ii) A beam of electrons, accelerated from rest through 500 V, passes undeflected through a region of crossed electric and magnetic fields. If B = 2.0 mT, find the speed of the electrons and the electric field. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) [2m]
items.orans:
(i) F = q[E + (v × B)]. [1]
With v, E and B mutually perpendicular and suitably oriented, the electric force qE and the magnetic force qvB act along the same line in opposite directions. The particle is undeflected when qE = qvB, i.e. v = E/B — independent of the charge and mass (this arrangement acts as a velocity selector). [1]
The magnetic force q(v × B) is always perpendicular to v, so its power F·v = 0; it does no work and cannot change the speed or kinetic energy, only the direction of motion. [1]
(ii) ½mv² = eV → v = √(2eV/m) = √(2 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 500/9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 1.33×10⁷ m/s. [1]
E = vB = 1.33×10⁷ × 2.0×10⁻³ ≈ 2.65×10⁴ V/m. [1]

items.q:
(A) (i) Using a ray diagram, show that for a concave mirror of small aperture the focal length is half the radius of curvature. State the Cartesian sign convention, and show that the linear magnification is m = −v/u. [3m]
(ii) A concave mirror is used to form an image of a candle flame on a wall 3.0 m from the candle. The image is five times as large as the flame. Find the distances of the candle and the wall from the mirror, and the focal length of the mirror. [2m]
items.ans:
(i) A ray parallel to the axis at height h strikes the mirror at M and reflects through F. CM is the normal (C is the centre of curvature), so the angle of incidence θ = ∠CMF = ∠MCP; triangle CMF is isosceles with FC = FM. For a small aperture, FM ≈ FP, so FP = PC/2, i.e. f = R/2. [1]
Sign convention: distances are measured from the pole; those in the direction of the incident light are positive, those opposite to it negative; heights above the axis are positive, below negative. [1]
An object AB and its real image A'B' form similar triangles with the pole P (ray reflected at P with equal angles): A'B'/AB = PB'/PB. With signs: −h'/h = −v/(−u) → m = h'/h = −v/u. [1]
(ii) m = −5 (real, inverted image on the wall): v = 5u, and the wall is farther from the mirror than the candle: |v| − |u| = 3.0 m → 4|u| = 3.0 → u = −0.75 m, v = −3.75 m. [1]
1/f = 1/v + 1/u = −1/3.75 − 1/0.75 = −1.6 m⁻¹ → f = −0.625 m (focal length 62.5 cm; R = 1.25 m). [1]
items.orq:
(B) (i) In Young's double-slit experiment, with slit separation d and screen distance D, derive expressions for the positions of the bright and dark fringes on the screen. Show that the bright and dark fringes are equally wide. [3m]
(ii) In such an experiment the slits are 0.50 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. The slits are illuminated by light containing two wavelengths, 450 nm and 600 nm. Find the fringe width for each wavelength and the least distance from the central maximum at which bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide. [2m]
items.orans:
(i) For a point P at distance x from the centre O of the screen, the path difference between waves from the two slits is S₂P − S₁P ≈ xd/D (for D ≫ d, x). [1]
Bright fringe: path difference = nλ → x_n = nλD/d (n = 0, 1, 2, …). Dark fringe: path difference = (2n + 1)λ/2 → x_n = (2n + 1)λD/2d. [1]
The distance between successive bright fringes is x(n+1) − x(n) = λD/d, and the same holds for successive dark fringes; so fringe width β = λD/d for both, independent of n (fringes are equally spaced). [1]
(ii) β₁ = 450×10⁻⁹ × 1.5/0.5×10⁻³ = 1.35 mm; β₂ = 600×10⁻⁹ × 1.5/0.5×10⁻³ = 1.8 mm. [1]
Coincidence: n₁(450) = n₂(600) → smallest integers n₁ = 4, n₂ = 3. x = 4 × 1.35 mm = 3 × 1.8 mm = 5.4 mm from the central maximum. [1]
